clause_title: Requirements for Money or Value Transfer Services
clause_content: (AML-CFT Decision Articles 26, 30) As part of a risk-based AML/CFT approach, FIs that enter into or maintain Business Relationships with Money or Value Transfer Services (MVTSs) should take adequate CDD measures that are commensurate with the risks involved (see Sections 6.3, Customer Due Diligence (CDD) Measures and 6.4, Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) Measures). Examples of measures that FIs should consider in this regard include, but are not limited to: * Ensuring that the MVTS is properly licensed or registered; in particular, when opening any accounts for Hawala Providers, FIs licensed by the Central Bank must physically check the original Hawala Provider registration certificate issued by the Central Bank and keep a copy thereof; * Obtaining information about and assessing the adequacy of the MVTS's AML/CFT policies, procedures and controls, including those related to Wire Transfers as stipulated in the relevant provisions of the AML-CFT Decision; * Obtaining the MVTS's list of agents, and identifying and assessing the associated ML/FT risks, especially with regard to high-risk countries or other identified high-risk factors; * Obtaining sufficient information about the MVTS's ownership and management structure (including taking into consideration the possibility of PEP involvement), the nature and scope of its business, the nature of its customer base, and the geographic areas in which it operates, so as to be in a position to identify, assess, and manage or mitigate the associated ML/FT risks. Fls that enter into or maintain relationships with MTVSs should also use a risk-based approach to determine the appropriate internal AML/CFT policies, procedures and controls Fls implement in relation to the risk assessment, risk classification, and the type and extent of CDD they perform on the MVTSs. The policies and procedures that Fls apply should be reasonable and proportionate to the risks involved, and should be adequately documented, senior management approved, and communicated to the relevant employees of the organisation.
interpretation:
The regulator expects FIs that establish or maintain Business Relationships with Money or Value Transfer Services (MVTS/Hawala providers) to apply specific enhanced, risk-based CDD measures tailored to this customer type, including: (1) verifying MVTS licensing/registration status with physical checking and copying of Hawala Provider registration certificates; (2) obtaining and assessing the MVTS's own AML/CFT policies, procedures and controls, including its wire transfer requirements; (3) obtaining the MVTS's agent list and assessing the ML/FT risk associated with those agents, particularly exposure to high-risk countries; (4) obtaining sufficient information on the MVTS's ownership/management structure (including any PEP involvement), nature and scope of business, customer base, and geographic areas of operation; and (5) documenting a risk-based internal policy/procedure specific to MVTS relationships (risk assessment, classification and CDD extent), approved by senior management and communicated to relevant staff.

The AML Manual addresses generic 'Financial Institutions relationships' CDD (registration/regulation check, reputation/integrity verification, obtaining documented DD process via questionnaire, obtaining written AML policies/controls, high-risk classification) but does not specifically address Money or Value Transfer Services (MVTS)/Hawala providers as a distinct customer category. Element-by-element: (1) Licensing/registration check with physical checking and copying of Hawala Provider registration certificates -- NOT covered (manual only mentions 'dealing only with registered and regulated companies' generically, no Hawala-specific certificate verification/copying requirement); (2) Obtaining/assessing MVTS's AML/CFT policies including wire transfer requirements -- PARTIALLY covered (generic reference to obtaining written policies/procedures/controls exists for 'Financial Institutions' but no specific mention of wire transfer requirements or MVTS applicability); (3) Obtaining the MVTS's agent list and assessing ML/FT risk of agents especially in high-risk countries -- NOT covered (no mention of agent lists anywhere in excerpts); (4) Obtaining sufficient information on MVTS ownership/management structure including PEP involvement, business nature/scope, customer base, geographic areas -- NOT covered specifically for MVTS (PEP procedures exist generally but not tied to MVTS ownership/management review); (5) Documented, senior-management approved, risk-based internal policy specific to MVTS CDD extent, communicated to employees -- NOT covered; no MVTS-specific policy is documented in the excerpts.

This can be achieved through filling the questionnaire for Financial Institutions.

• Establishing that the company has in place written policies, procedures and internal controls to address the risks of its business being used as a vehicle for illegal activities, including the establishment of management controls to prevent the involvement of the insurance company in money laundering and terrorist financing schemes. clause_content: Non-Profit Organisations (NPOs) can often pose increased risks in regard to money laundering, the financing of terrorism, and the financing of illegal organisations. As part of an effective risk-based approach to AML/CFT, FIs that enter into or maintain Business Relationships with NPOs should take adequate CDD measures that are commensurate with the risks involved (see Sections 6.3, Customer Due Diligence (CDD) Measures and 6.4, Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) Measures). Examples of measures that FIs should consider include, but are not limited to: • Ensuring that the NPO (including charitable) is properly licensed or registered. In particular, when opening any accounts to collect or receive donations for any entity, FIs licensed by the Central Bank must obtain a letter from the Minister of Community Development or her authorized representative or from the head of the local authority concerned with the organisation of donations or his/her authorized representative, which allows opening of such accounts. Note that conducting financial transfers out of the UAE through these accounts must be done via the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. • Obtaining information about and assessing the adequacy of the NPO's AML/CFT policies, procedures and controls; • Obtaining sufficient information about the NPO's legal, regulatory and supervisory status, including requirements relating to regulatory disclosure, accounting, financial reporting and audit (especially where community/social or religious/cultural organisations are involved, and when those organisations are based, or have significant operations, in jurisdictions that are unfamiliar or in which transparency or access to information may be limited for any reason); • Obtaining sufficient information about the NPO's ownership and management structure (including taking into consideration the possibility of PEP involvement); the nature and scope of its activities; the nature of its donor base, as well as of that of the beneficiaries of its activities and programmes; and the geographic areas in which it operates, so as to be in a position to identify, assess, and manage or mitigate the associated ML/FT risks; • Performing thorough background checks (including but not limited to the use of internet searches, public databases, or subscription information aggregation services) on the NPO's key persons, such as senior management, branch or field managers, major donors and major beneficiaries, to screen for possible matches with targeted and other international financial sanctions lists, indications of criminal activity (including financial crime), or other adverse information. Fls that enter into or maintain relationships with NPOs should also use a risk-based approach to determine the appropriate internal AML/CFT policies, procedures and controls the Fls implement in relation to the risk assessment, risk classification, and the type and extent of CDD they perform on NPOs. The policies and procedures that Fls apply should be reasonable and proportionate to the risks involved, and should be adequately documented, senior management approved, and communicated to the relevant employees of the organisation.
interpretation:
The regulator expects FIs to have specific, documented, risk-based CDD policies and procedures for Non-Profit Organisation (NPO) customers, covering: (1) verifying proper licensing/registration of the NPO, including specific documentary requirements for donation-collection accounts (Minister of Community Development letter) and outbound transfers (via Ministry of Foreign Affairs); (2) obtaining and assessing the NPO's own AML/CFT policies and controls; (3) obtaining sufficient information on the NPO's legal/regulatory/supervisory status (disclosure, accounting, reporting, audit requirements); (4) obtaining sufficient information on ownership/management structure including PEP involvement, nature/scope of activities, donor/beneficiary base, and geographic areas of operation; (5) performing background/sanctions checks on key persons (senior management, branch/field managers, major donors/beneficiaries); and (6) ensuring this risk-based NPO CDD framework is documented, approved by senior management, and communicated to relevant staff.

None of the provided excerpts of the Internal AML Manual contain any NPO-specific CDD provisions. Element-by-element review: (1) NPO licensing/registration verification, donation-account Minister of Community Development letter requirement, and outbound transfer via Ministry of Foreign Affairs -- not covered anywhere in the excerpts. (2) Obtaining/assessing the NPO's own AML/CFT policies/controls -- not covered (only general Financial Institution due diligence questionnaire is mentioned for FI relationships, not NPOs). (3) Obtaining information on NPO's legal/regulatory/supervisory status (disclosure/accounting/reporting/audit requirements) -- not covered. (4) Information on ownership/management structure including PEP involvement, activity nature/scope, donor/beneficiary base, geographic areas -- not covered; general PEP and CDD/EDD sections (pp.26-29, 42-43) address PEPs generally but do not reference NPOs specifically. (5) Background/sanctions checks on key persons (senior management, branch/field managers, major donors/beneficiaries) of NPOs -- not covered; general sanctions screening exists (pp.24-25) but no NPO-specific key-person check requirement. (6) Documented, senior-management-approved, communicated risk-based NPO policy -- not evidenced. The manual addresses general CDD/EDD, PEPs, high-risk customers, and Financial Institution relationships, but contains no distinct NPO risk-based CDD framework as required by this clause.

clause_content: (AML-CFT Decision Articles 4.3, 5, 10) In keeping with a risk-based approach to CDD, under certain circumstances and in the absence of a ML/FT suspicion, FIs are only permitted to exercise simplified customer due diligence measures (SDD) with regard to customers identified as low-risk through an adequate analysis of risks. SDD generally involves a more lenient application of certain aspects of CDD measures, including elements as: * A reduction in verification requirements with regard to customer or Beneficial Owner identification; * Fewer and less detailed inquiries in regard to the purpose of the Business Relationship, the nature of the customer's business, the customer's source of funds, and the purpose of individual transactions; * More limited supervision of the Business Relationship, including less frequent monitoring of transactions, and less frequent review/updating of customer due diligence information. Specifically, the AML-CFT Decision permits the application of SDD in the following circumstances: * Identified low-risk customers. When the customer or Beneficial Owner is identified as posing a low risk of ML/FT, FIs are permitted to complete the verification of their identity after the establishment of a Business Relationship under the conditions specified in the relevant provisions of the AML-CFT Decision. In this regard, FIs are required to implement appropriate and effective measures to control the risks of ML/FT, including the risks in regard to the customer or Beneficial Owner benefitting from the Business Relationship prior to the completion of the verification process. Examples of such measures which FIs may consider taking in this regard are, among others: - Holding funds in suspense or in escrow until the verification of the identity is completed; - Making the completion of verification of the identity a condition precedent to the closing of a transaction. It should be noted that the provision allowing a relaxation of the timing for the completion of the identity verification procedures does not imply that FIs are permitted to establish a Business Relationship without any customer identification at all. On the contrary, in all cases, the basic identification information in relation to the customer (whether a natural or legal person or arrangement) should be obtained; however under the specified conditions, FIs are permitted to establish the Business Relationship prior to the completion of the verification process, which may include such steps as: obtaining appropriate supporting documentation, certifications or attestations, when necessary (for example, as regards the corporate documents of a legal person); or obtaining all the necessary information related to the relevant parties of a legal person or Legal Arrangement, such as Beneficial Owners, settlors, trustees or executors, protectors, beneficiaries, or other controlling persons. * Listed companies. FIs are exempted from identifying and verifying the identity of any shareholder, partner or Beneficial Owner of a legal person under the conditions specified in the relevant provisions of the AML-CFT Decision. Namely: - When the relevant information on the shareholder, partner or Beneficial Owner is obtained from reliable sources; and - When the customer, or the owner holding the controlling interest of the customer, is a company listed on a regulated stock exchange subject to adequate disclosure and transparency requirements related to Beneficial Ownership; or when the customer, or the owner holding the controlling interest of a legal entity customer, is the majority-held subsidiary of such a listed company. Without prejudice to the above, in the case of foreign stock exchanges, FIs should take steps to adequately assess and document the relevant disclosure and transparency requirements related to Beneficial Ownership, and to ensure that they are at least equivalent to those of the UAE. In addition, FIs should be aware that, regardless of the exemption mentioned above, FIs are required with respect to listed companies to verify that any person purporting to act on behalf of the customer is so authorised, and verify the identity of that person. As part of their overall AML/CFT framework, FIs should use a risk-based approach to determine the internal policies, procedures and controls they implement in connection with the application of SDD procedures. Examples of some of the factors they should consider when developing their risk-based policies include: * the ML/FT risks identified in the ML/TF business risk assessment, especially with regard to low-risk categories of customers; * Circumstances, timing, and composition in regard to the application of SDD measures; * Frequency of reviews and updates in relation to customer SDD information; * Extent and frequency of ongoing supervision of the Business Relationship and monitoring of transactions in relation to customers to which SDD measures are applied. Such policies, procedures and methodologies should be reasonable and proportionate to the risks involved, and, in formulating them, Fls should consider the results of both the NRA and any Topical Risk Assessment and their own ML/FT business risk assessments. Commensurate with the nature and size of the Fls' businesses, the policies, procedures and methodologies should also be documented, approved by senior management, and communicated at the appropriate levels of the organisation.
interpretation:
The regulator expects FIs to have a documented, risk-based SDD framework covering: (1) deferred verification for identified low-risk customers with compensating controls (e.g., escrow/suspense of funds, verification as condition precedent) while still capturing basic ID info and information on relevant parties upfront; (2) an exemption from verifying shareholders/BOs of listed companies from regulated exchanges with adequate disclosure (including equivalence assessment for foreign exchanges) while still verifying persons acting on the company's behalf; and (3) internal SDD policies/procedures/controls that are risk-based (informed by NRA/BRA), specify circumstances/timing/composition of SDD application and review/update frequency and monitoring extent, and are documented, senior-management approved, and communicated.

Element 1 (deferred verification for identified low-risk customers with compensating controls such as escrow/suspense of funds or verification as condition precedent, while still obtaining basic ID info upfront and info on relevant parties): NOT covered - the manual only states SDD can be applied to low-risk customers without violating regulatory requirements, but does not describe deferred verification timing, compensating risk-control measures, or the requirement to still obtain basic identification/relevant-party information upfront. Element 2 (listed company exemption from verifying shareholders/BOs, with equivalence assessment for foreign exchanges, and still verifying persons acting on the company's behalf): NOT covered anywhere in the excerpts. Element 3 (internal SDD policies/procedures/controls that are risk-based per NRA/BRA, specifying circumstances/timing/composition of SDD application, review/update frequency, monitoring extent, documented, senior-management approved, and communicated): NOT covered - the manual gives only a generic one-line statement on SDD applicability with no documented procedure, approval, or communication process specified.
policy_extract: Simplified due diligence measures can be applied when the risks of money laundering and terrorist financing is low and there aren’t any suspicions of money laundering or terrorist financing activities.
Simplified measures can be applied with low risk customers including measures to identify and verify the identity of the customer without violating any regulatory requirements.

clause_content: (AML-CFT Decision Articles 19) Under certain conditions, the AML-CFT Decision permits FIs to rely on third parties to undertake the required CDD measures, including those measures specifically laid out in regard to identified high-risk countries (see [Section 6.4.3, Requirements for High-Risk Countries]), with the responsibility for the validity of the measures resting directly with the FIs. Among the conditions set forth in the AML-CFT Decision concerning the reliance on third parties, it is stipulated that FIs shall: "Ensure that the third party is regulated and supervised, and adheres to the CDD measures towards Customers and record-keeping provisions of the present Decision." In order to fulfil this obligation, FIs that rely on third parties to undertake CDD measures on their behalf should implement adequate measures, in keeping with the nature and size of their businesses, to ensure the third party's adherence to the requirements of the AML-CFT Law and the AML-CFT Decision in relation to CDD measures. Examples of such measures include: * Clearly defined procedures for determining the adequacy of a third-party's CDD and record-keeping measures, including the evaluation of such factors as the comprehensiveness and quality of its AML/CFT policies, procedures and controls; the number of personnel dedicated to CDD; and its audit and/or quality assurance policies in regard to CDD. In this regard, FIs are advised that tools such as questionnaires, scorecards, and on-site visits may be useful in evaluating the adequacy of a third party's adherence. * Service-level agreements, clearly setting out the roles and responsibilities of the FI and the third party and specifying the nature of the CDD and record-keeping requirements to be fulfilled. * Procedures for the certification by third parties of documents and other records pertaining to the CDD measures undertaken. In addition to the above, when relying on foreign third parties for the undertaking of CDD measures, FIs should take steps to ensure that the AML/CFT regulatory and supervisory framework under which the third party operates is at least equivalent to that of the State. This means that FIs should ensure that the third party is regulated and supervised for AML/CFT purposes, and adheres to the equivalent CDD and record-keeping measures. Whichever methods are utilized to ensure the adherence of third parties to the statutory CDD and record-keeping requirements, FIs should document and periodically review them for effectiveness. Reliance on a third party refers to an FI's reliance on a third party of the entire or part of the CDD process as well as reliance on a third party when to introducing business. FIs should therefore take adequate steps to satisfy themselves that copies of identification data and other relevant documentation relating to the CDD requirements will be made available from the third party upon request without delay. This includes the identification and verification of the identity of customers and Beneficial Owners, beneficiaries or controlling persons of legal entities or arrangements, as well as the investigation and assembly of other relevant customer documents, information and data, as per the statutory CDD and record-keeping requirements. Nevertheless, FIs remain ultimately responsible for the outcome of the CDD process. Furthermore, FIs should themselves assess the risks of the customer, including the customer's risk profile. FIs should thus document their rationale for the assignment of relevant customer risk classifications, as well as their analysis of the CDD information obtained from the third parties. Moreover, FIs remain themselves responsible for conducting ongoing due diligence on the business relationship and scrutiny of transactions undertaken throughout the course of that relationship. For the purpose of this guidance, it is important to note that FIs are expected to use documents, data or information from reliable and independent sources in carrying out their CDD obligations, which include, among other things, verifying the identity of customers and Beneficial Owners, beneficiaries or controlling persons of legal entities or arrangements. Reliable and independent sources may include, but are not necessarily limited to, official bodies such as Competent Authorities, governmental departments or agencies, governmental or state-sponsored business registries, public utilities or similar official enterprises; as well as non-official organisations, such as publicly accessible free or subscription information aggregation services, credit reporting agencies, and others. Fls are reminded that simply obtaining CDD documents and supporting information from reliable and independent sources during the course of performing their own CDD procedures is not necessarily considered as reliance on a third party. On occasion that Fls during the course of carrying out their own CDD procedures, receive certain documents, information or data from a third-party, Fls should obtain evidence of the third party's regulatory and supervisory status and good standing, and they should also consider obtaining the third party's certification that any CDD documents provided by them (such as identification documents, proof of address, or documents corroborating a customer's source of funds) are true copies of the originals.
interpretation:
The regulator expects FIs that rely on third parties for CDD to: (1) ensure third party is regulated/supervised and adheres to CDD/record-keeping requirements; (2) implement defined procedures/tools (questionnaires, scorecards, on-site visits) to assess third-party CDD adequacy including policies, staffing, and audit/QA; (3) use service-level agreements defining roles/responsibilities; (4) have procedures for third-party certification of documents; (5) for foreign third parties, ensure equivalence of regulatory/supervisory framework to UAE standards; (6) document and periodically review the adequacy assessment methods; (7) ensure CDD documentation is obtainable without delay; (8) retain ultimate responsibility for CDD outcomes, perform own customer risk assessment, document risk classification rationale, and maintain ongoing due diligence/monitoring responsibility; (9) recognize that using reliable/independent sources for CDD is not necessarily 'reliance' but still requires evidence of the source's regulatory standing/certification of true copies.

Element-by-element review: (1) Third party must be regulated/supervised and adhere to CDD/record-keeping - COVERED (manual lists eligible third parties and FATF-equivalent supervision requirement, pp.35-36). (2) Clearly defined procedures/tools (questionnaires, scorecards, on-site visits) to assess third-party CDD adequacy including policies, personnel numbers, audit/QA - NOT COVERED; manual does not describe any assessment tools, scorecards, or on-site visit procedures for vetting third-party CDD programs. (3) Service-level agreements defining roles/responsibilities - NOT COVERED; no mention of SLAs. (4) Procedures for third-party certification of documents as true copies - PARTIALLY COVERED; manual states DIFC must take 'adequate steps to satisfy itself that certified copies... will be available... without delay' but does not detail a certification procedure. (5) Foreign third-party equivalence assessment - COVERED via factors listed (mutual evaluations, FATF membership, contextual factors, cooperation arrangements). (6) Document and periodically review methods ensuring third-party adherence - NOT COVERED; no periodic review cadence or documentation requirement specified for the assessment methodology itself. (7) Steps to ensure CDD documentation available without delay - COVERED. (8) FI remains ultimately responsible for CDD outcomes and performs own risk assessment - COVERED (manual states DIFC remains responsible and must perform CDD itself for deficiencies), but documentation of risk classification rationale and ongoing due diligence responsibility while relying on third party is not explicitly addressed in this section. (9) Distinction between reliance and use of reliable/independent sources, with evidence of regulatory standing - PARTIALLY COVERED; general KYC section mentions using 'reliable and independent sources' but does not elaborate on obtaining evidence of the source's regulatory standing or certification distinct from third-party reliance.
policy_extract: DIFC may rely on the following third parties to conduct one or more elements of CDD on its behalf: 1. A DFSA regulated firm; 2. A law firm, notary, or other independent legal business, accounting firm or audit firm in another jurisdiction; 3. A financial institution; or 4. A member of its Group.

Where DIFC relies on a third party listed above, it may only do so if and to the following extent: a. It immediately obtains the necessary CDD information from the third party; b. It takes adequate steps to satisfy itself that certified copies of the documents used to undertake the relevant elements of CDD will be available from the third party on request without delay; c. If the third party is in another country, then it is subject to requirements in relation to customer due diligence and record keeping which meet the standards set out in the FATF Recommendations; and Supervised for compliance with those requirements in a manner that meets the standards for regulation and supervision set out in the FATF Recommendations

When making assessment to see if requirements, supervision or regulation in another jurisdiction meet FATF standards, DIFC must take into account factors including, among other things: a. Mutual evaluations, assessment reports or follow-up reports published by FATF, the IMF, the World Bank, the OECD or other International Organisations; b. Membership of FATF or other international or regional groups such as the MENAFATF or the Gulf Co-operation Council; c. Contextual factors such as political stability or the level of corruption in the jurisdiction (d) evidence of recent criticism of the jurisdiction...

If DIFC is not reasonably satisfied with the CDD undertaken by a third party, DIFC must perform the CDD itself with respect to any deficiencies identified. Notwithstanding reliance on a third party, it should be noted that DIFC remains responsible for compliance with, and liable for any failure to meet, / the CDD requirements in the DFSA AML module.

clause_content: Under the AML/CFT legal and regulatory framework of the UAE, all FIs are obliged to promptly report to the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU) suspicious transactions and any additional information required in relation to them, when there are suspicions, or reasonable grounds to suspect, that the proceeds are related to a crime, or to the attempt or intention to use funds or proceeds for the purpose of committing, concealing or benefitting from a crime. FIs are required to put in place and update indicators that can be used to identify possible suspicious transactions. In order to fulfil these obligations, FIs should implement adequate internal policies, procedures and controls in relation to the identification and the immediate reporting of suspicious transactions. The following sub-sections provide additional guidance in this regard.
interpretation: The regulator expects FIs to: (1) promptly report suspicious transactions and related information to the FIU when there are reasonable grounds to suspect proceeds relate to a crime or funds are intended for criminal use/concealment/benefit; (2) develop and update indicators to identify possible suspicious transactions; and (3) implement adequate internal policies, procedures and controls for identifying and immediately reporting suspicious transactions.
policy_extract: Upon receiving a suspicious transaction report, the department must act immediately to conduct the necessary investigations, review the transactions, request the necessary documents and information, and take the appropriate decision for the case. All suspicious transactions, including attempts to conduct a transaction, must be reported regardless of the amount of the transaction. Regulatory procedures should be followed in the event that the decision to report the suspected transaction to the Financial Investigation / Intelligence Unit (FIU).

The department should lay down procedures for investigations and reporting of Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing that guarantee the effectiveness and efficiency of investigations. The procedures must also include a mechanism for keeping records and confidential arrangements.
All employees must review the Indicators of Suspected Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing' Guidelines issued by the Department.

The department should pay special attention to monitoring all transactions, and the use of the automated systems to facilitate the monitoring of transactions by detecting abnormal activities, alerts and notifications that define unusual transactions or activities.

In the event that there are any doubts that the financial transaction will be used for unlawful purposes - such as terrorist financing transactions - then it is necessary to stop the transaction without tipping-off or notifying the customer of any suspicion.
External SAR: The MLRO must lodge the SAR with the FIU via GoAML as soon as practicable and without delay
Internal SAR: The Firm's Employee must promptly notify the MLRO and provide all the relevant details
Submit a SAR within a reasonable timeframe of identifying the suspicious activity;

clause_title: Role of the Financial Intelligence Unit
interpretation:
This clause is primarily descriptive of the FIU's own role, mandate and functions as a national agency (receiving/analysing STRs, disseminating to Competent Authorities, cooperating with foreign FIUs, maintaining protocols, operating GoAML, producing trend/typology reports) -- most of this is regulator/FIU-facing content describing the FIU itself, and has no implementing counterpart expected in a bank's internal AML manual. However, embedded within the clause is one bank-facing operational obligation: 'FIs shall register on GoAML, maintain active registration, and new licensed FIs must register immediately upon obtaining their license.' The bank's internal manual should reflect this registration/maintenance obligation as it is a direct requirement on the institution.

Element-level review: (1) FIU's core national-agency functions (receiving/analysing STRs and disseminating to Competent Authorities, receiving reports from Federal Customs Authority, requesting info from Competent Authorities, coordinating with Supervisory Authorities on STR quality, sending data to Law Enforcement/judiciary, exchanging info with foreign FIU counterparts, maintaining operational protocols, trend analysis and typology report distribution) -- this is regulator-facing descriptive content about the FIU's own mandate; no bank-side implementation is expected, and its absence from the internal manual is not a gap. (2) 'FIs shall register on GoAML, maintain active registration, and new licensed FIs must register immediately upon obtaining their license' -- the internal manual references reporting suspicious transactions to FIU 'through GoAml' (pp.14, 19) confirming GoAML is used as the filing channel, but it does not explicitly state an obligation to register on GoAML, maintain active registration status, or register immediately upon obtaining a new license. This specific registration/maintenance requirement is missing in the internal document.
policy_extract: Sending communications, detailed studies and copies of documents of suspicious cases after MLRO approval to the Financial Investigation Unit (FIU).

All suspicious transactions that are made by clients or employees of the DIFC, should be reported to the department immediately by all business units and departments within DIFC to take the necessary measures, and inform the Financial Investigation Unit (FIU) through GoAml.
Report cases of suspicion to the Financial Investigation Unit (FIU) through GoAml.

clause_title: Processing of STRs by the FIU
clause_content:
A core function of the FIU is to conduct operational analysis on STRs and information received from FIs, DNFBPs, as well as from Competent Authorities, and to support the investigations of Law Enforcement Authorities. It does so by identifying specific targets (such as persons, funds, or criminal networks) and by following the trail of specific transactions in order to determine the linkages between those targets and the possible proceeds of crime, money laundering, predicate offences and terrorist financing.
Upon the receipt of STRs or information from reporting institutions or other sources, the FIU assesses the information, prioritises the risk, and performs its own analyses using a variety of information sources and analytical techniques.
In certain cases, the FIU may request additional information from the reporting entity, Competent Authorities, or even from other FIs which also have a business relationship with the subject of its analysis or investigation, through the Integrated Enquiries Management System (IEMS). Upon concluding its analysis or investigation, the FIU may disseminate information about the case to Law Enforcement Authorities or foreign FIUs, and may, at its own discretion, also provide feedback to the reporting entity in the form of instructions regarding required actions to be taken, or recommendations and guidance.
In addition to the above, the FIU also performs strategic analysis, using data aggregated from the STRs and other information it receives, including from national and international Competent Authorities and FIUs of other countries, to identify trends and patterns relating to ML/FT. As a result of this analysis, the FIU may from time to time disseminate enhanced due diligence and fraud alerts to FIs as a preventive measure, and may also disseminate information to FIs about prevalent or new and emerging ML/FT typologies, or other specific risks which FIs should take into consideration.
interpretation: This clause describes the FIU's own internal operational and strategic analysis processes for STRs -- how the FIU (a government body) analyses, prioritizes, disseminates and provides feedback on reports it receives. This is regulator/authority-facing descriptive content about the FIU's own functions, not an obligation imposed on the reporting bank. There is no implementing counterpart expected in the bank's internal AML Manual other than the bank's role as a reporting entity (submitting STRs, responding to FIU inquiries, and receiving/acting on feedback), which is a separate matter from the FIU's internal analytical process described here.
policy_extract: Upon receiving a suspicious transaction report, the department must act immediately to conduct the necessary investigations, review the transactions, request the necessary documents and information, and take the appropriate decision for the case.

DFSA Branch Compliance is responsible for receiving and responding to DFSA AML&CTF inquiries in relation to specific names, entities and transactions, which banks are required to search for any relationship/ account and to report back to DFSA with detailed information including copies of account opening documentation, statements, source media, etc.

interpretation:
The regulator requires the FI's policy to define a suspicious transaction in the full statutory sense: any transaction, attempted transaction, or funds that there are reasonable grounds to suspect (not proof) constitute, in whole or part and irrespective of amount or timing, proceeds of crime, or are related to or intended for use in ML/FT/illegal organisation financing offences. The definition must clarify that (a) reasonable suspicion alone is sufficient - there is no need to prove a predicate offence or the illicit source of funds, or to have actual knowledge of underlying criminal activity, and (b) the reporting obligation covers attempted, unexecuted/incomplete, and past transactions later found (upon review) to give rise to reasonable grounds for suspicion - not only completed or pending transactions.

Element 1 (transactions/attempted transactions/funds suspected as proceeds of crime, or related to/intended for ML/FT/illegal org financing, regardless of amount): Partially covered - the manual states 'All suspicious transactions, including attempts to conduct a transaction, must be reported regardless of the amount of the transaction' and references ML/TF suspicion, but does not explicitly extend this to 'illegal organisation financing crimes' or explicitly state 'funds' (not just transactions) fall within scope, and does not explicitly say 'in whole or part' or 'regardless of...timing'. Element 2 (reasonable grounds suffice; no need to prove predicate offence, illicit source, or have actual knowledge): Not covered - the manual never states that mere reasonable grounds/suspicion is sufficient without proof of a predicate offence, illicit source of funds, or knowledge of underlying criminal activity (this concept appears only in the glossary describing the money laundering offence definition under Federal Decree-Law No. 20/2018, not in the context of what constitutes/must be reported as a suspicious transaction). Element 3 (attempted, unexecuted, and past transactions found upon review to give rise to suspicion must be reported): Partially covered - attempted transactions are explicitly captured, but there is no explicit mention that past/completed transactions reviewed later and found to raise suspicion must also be reported.
policy_extract: All suspicious transactions, including attempts to conduct a transaction, must be reported regardless of the amount of the transaction.

All concerned employees must be diligent when initiating transactions or when reviewing customer transactions in order to know if there are any unusual transaction that exceed the customer's usual pattern or that the transaction does not match the customer's information. Upon suspecting any transactions, they must report immediately to the department without notifying the suspect or any other party since this is a violation of the regulations and the responsible party will be held accountable.
In case of suspicion that the financial transaction may involve money laundering, the employee in charge must not tip-off or notify the customer of any information.

interpretation:
The regulator expects FIs to: (1) establish and maintain indicators for identifying suspicious transactions, updating them per FIU instructions, typology developments and NRA/risk assessment results; (2) set internal policies/procedures/controls for indicator identification, implementation, updating, and STR evaluation, covering roles/responsibilities, IT/operational procedures, and staff training; (3) ensure adequate processes and dedicated experienced staff for alert investigation with documented investigation and closure/reporting decisions; (4) report to the FIU immediately once suspicion becomes clear, showing continuous action; (5) have a defined reporting procedure that includes examining earlier/related transactions and reconsidering risk profiles; (6) apply no minimum threshold for reporting; (7) treat presence of a non-obligatory indicator as requiring immediate investigation considering product/service and customer risk context; (8) provide example typologies of suspicious transactions for staff awareness; (9) require selection of an appropriate reporting reason in GoAML.

Element-by-element review: (1) Indicators for suspicious transactions - PARTIALLY covered: manual references 'Indicators of Suspected Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Guidelines' but does not describe a process for updating these indicators based on FIU instructions, typology developments, or NRA/business risk assessment results. (2) Internal policies for indicator identification/implementation/updating, roles/responsibilities, IT/operational procedures, staff training - PARTIALLY covered: general monitoring and training sections exist but no explicit linkage of indicator design/update process to organisational roles, IT systems, and training specifically for indicator management. (3) Adequate processes and dedicated experienced staff for alert investigation with documented investigation/closure decisions - COVERED: 'the department must act immediately to conduct the necessary investigations... and take the appropriate decision for the case.' (4) Immediate reporting to FIU once suspicion is clear, demonstrating continuous action - PARTIALLY covered: reporting to FIU via GoAML is mentioned but 'immediate and continuous action from the alert' language and urgency emphasis not explicit. (5) Defined reporting procedure including examining earlier/related transactions and reconsidering risk profiles - NOT COVERED: no mention of examining earlier/related transactions or reconsidering customer risk profile during investigation. (6) No minimum threshold for reporting - COVERED: 'must be reported regardless of the amount of the transaction.' (7) Presence of non-obligatory indicator requiring immediate investigation considering product/service and customer risk context - NOT explicitly covered. (8) Example typologies of suspicious transactions provided - NOT found in excerpts (reference is only to external 'Indicators' guideline document, not internal list of example transaction types). (9) GoAML requirement to select at least one appropriate reporting reason - NOT COVERED: manual mentions GoAML reporting but not the requirement to select a reporting reason from the menu. Overall, several core elements (indicator update cycle, risk-profile reconsideration, examining earlier/related transactions, example typologies, GoAML reason selection) are missing or not evidenced in the excerpts.

All suspicious transactions, including attempts to conduct a transaction, must be reported regardless of the amount of the transaction. Regulatory procedures should be followed in the event that the decision to report the suspected transaction to the Financial Investigation Unit (FIU) through GoAml.

The department should lay down procedures for investigations and reporting of Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing that guarantee the effectiveness and efficiency of investigations. The procedures must also include a mechanism for keeping records and confidential arrangements.
document_reference: Internal AML Manual 290626.pdf, pp.45-47 (Monitoring Financial Transactions; Investigations and Reporting)

clause_content:
Fls are obliged to report transactions to the FIU without delay when there are suspicions, or reasonable grounds to suspect, that the proceeds are related to a crime, or to the attempt or intention to use funds or proceeds for the purpose of committing, concealing or benefitting from a crime. There is no minimum reporting threshold; all suspicious transactions, including attempted transactions, should be reported regardless of the amount of the transaction. There is also no statute of limitations with regard to when the possible crimes or the suspicious transaction took place.
Under federal law and regulations, whether the FI operates in the mainland UAE or in a Financial or Commercial Free Zone, the designated Competent Authority for the reporting of suspicious transactions is the FIU.
Failure to – immediately – report a suspicious transaction, whether intentionally or by gross negligence, is a federal crime. Any person, including FIs or their managers and employees, who fails to perform their statutory obligation to report a suspicion of money laundering, or the financing of terrorism or of illegal organisations, is liable to a fine of no less than AED100,000 and no more than AED1,000,000 and/or imprisonment.
There are no exemptions from the statutory reporting requirement provided for FIs under the AML-CFT Law or AML-CFT Cabinet Decision.
interpretation:
The regulator requires FIs to: (1) report suspicious transactions to the FIU without delay upon suspicion or reasonable grounds relating to crime proceeds/intent; (2) apply no minimum reporting threshold; (3) apply no statute of limitations on reporting obligation; (4) recognize the FIU as the designated Competent Authority for STR reporting regardless of mainland/Free Zone status; (5) understand and communicate the criminal liability (fine AED100,000-1,000,000 and/or imprisonment) for failure to report intentionally or by gross negligence; and (6) apply no exemptions from the reporting requirement.

Element-level review: (1) Immediate reporting to FIU upon suspicion - COVERED (pp.14, 40: 'report them immediately to the department...inform the FIU through GoAml'; 'DIFC Branch Compliance shall report the case to...FIU'). (2) No minimum reporting threshold - COVERED (p.38: 'must be reported regardless of the amount of the transaction'). (3) No statute of limitations on reporting - NOT COVERED; the manual does not state that there is no time-bar or limitation period on the obligation to report once suspicion arises. (4) FIU as designated Competent Authority regardless of mainland/Free Zone - PARTIALLY COVERED; the manual references reporting to FIU via GoAML and DFSA notification but does not explicitly state that FIU is the Competent Authority irrespective of mainland/Free Zone status of the reporting entity. (5) Criminal liability for failure to report (specific fine range AED100,000-1,000,000 and/or imprisonment) - NOT COVERED; the manual only generally references 'internal disciplinary procedures as well as criminal prosecution and/or external organizational penalties' without citing the specific statutory fine range or imprisonment consequence tied to failure to report. (6) No exemptions from reporting requirement - NOT COVERED; not explicitly stated in the manual.
policy_extract: All suspicious transactions that are made by clients or employees of the  DIFC, should be reported to the department immediately by all business units and departments within  DIFC to take the necessary measures, and inform the Financial Investigation Unit (FIU) through GoAml.

All suspicious transactions, including attempts to conduct a transaction, must be reported regardless of the amount of the transaction. Regulatory procedures should be followed in the event that the decision to report the suspected transaction to the Financial Investigation / Intelligence

DIFC Branch Compliance shall report the case to Anti Money Laundering Suspicious Cases Unit (FIU) in Central Bank UAE with a copy to DFSA via GoAML, if they conclude that the transaction is suspicious.
Applying internal disciplinary procedures as well as criminal prosecution and/or external organizational penalties in the event of failure to follow any AML/CTF or Sanctions procedures.

clause_title: Procedures for the Reporting of Suspicious Transactions
interpretation:
The regulator expects FIs to have documented, senior-management approved procedures for STR reporting via GoAML, effected by the compliance officer (MLRO), covering: (1) reporting via GoAML or FIU-approved means; (2) compliance officer's duty to review/scrutinize records and decide whether to report, with documented reasons if not reporting; (3) confidentiality maintenance; (4) internal reporting procedures from staff to compliance officer including: (a) internal investigation policy prior to STR filing, (b) conditions/timing/methods of internal reporting, (c) content/format requirements for internal reports, (d) confidentiality/data protection controls, (e) post-filing procedures for additional information/follow-up/relationship handling, (f) compliance officer decision-making policies, and other appropriate conditions; and (5) documentation, senior management approval, and appropriate communication of these procedures.

Element-by-element assessment: (1) Reporting via GoAML - COVERED ('all Relevant Persons to register on the GoAML system and submit SARs electronically'). (2) Compliance officer/MLRO duty to review and decide whether to report - PARTIALLY COVERED (MLRO 'investigates the suspicious activity and considers whether an SAR should be lodged'), but no explicit requirement to document reasons when deciding NOT to report/maintain the transaction internally instead of filing - this is missing in the Manual. (3) Confidentiality - COVERED ('Report confidentially without involving unrelated people', tipping-off provisions on p.14/41). (4) Internal investigation policy prior to STR filing - PARTIALLY COVERED; MLRO 'investigates' but no detailed internal investigation policy/procedure is documented. (5) Conditions/timing/methods for internal reporting - PARTIALLY COVERED ('promptly notify the MLRO') but no specific timing standards or methods (e.g., form, escalation channel) beyond referencing an STR form generally. (6) Content/format requirements for internal reports - NOT CLEARLY COVERED; only a general STR form is mentioned, no detailed content/format standard for internal notifications is shown in excerpts. (7) Confidentiality/data protection controls for internal reporting specifically - PARTIALLY COVERED via general tipping-off/confidentiality provisions but no dedicated data protection control language. (8) Post-filing procedures for additional information/follow-up/business relationship handling - NOT COVERED in excerpts; no procedure describing how to handle the business relationship or respond to FIU follow-up requests after STR filing. (9) Compliance officer decision-making policy - PARTIALLY COVERED (MLRO has sole authority to decide) but no documented decision-making criteria/policy. (10) Documentation, senior management approval, and communication of these procedures - NOT EXPLICITLY SHOWN; no evidence that the internal reporting procedure itself was senior-management approved and communicated as a discrete policy.
policy_extract: From 27 June 2019, the FIU requires all Relevant Persons to register on the GoAML system and submit SARs electronically through this portal.
Internal SAR: The Firm's Employee must promptly notify the MLRO and provide all the relevant details
Investigation: The MLRO investigates the suspicious activity and considers whether an SAR should be lodged with the FIU of the Central Bank of the UAE via GoAML
External SAR: The MLRO must lodge the SAR with the FIU via GoAML as soon as practicable and without delay

Making an external SAR to the FIU and notifying the DFSA is the sole responsibility of the MLRO.  It is their decision to make independently and is not subject to the consent or approval of any other Person
Report confidentially without involving unrelated people as it could alert the customer and be considered as ‘tipping off’;

The department maintains a record of all reports related to Anti-Money Laundering and Counterterrorist Financing, including investigation reports and studies related to cases of suspected money laundering, terrorist financing and sanctions.

clause_content:
Fls are obliged to report STRs to the FIU without delay. Since it is the responsibility of the designated AML/CFT compliance officer to “review, scrutinise and study records, receive data concerning suspicious transactions, and take decisions to either notify the FIU or maintain the transaction,” (see Section 8.1, Compliance Officer) it follows that the STRs should be immediately reported once the suspicious nature of the transaction becomes clear. This means that the internal reporting of suspicious transactions to the compliance officer should be done directly once the suspicion or reasonable grounds for suspicion are established, and immediately the designated AML/CFT compliance officer has confirmed that the transaction (whether pending, in progress, or past) is suspicious, it should be reported.
Without prejudice to the above, FIs should note that, with the exception of any obligatory indicators for which immediate reporting to the FIU is required by the relevant Competent Authorities, some potentially suspicious transactions or indicators of suspicion may require a degree of internal investigation before a suspicion or reasonable grounds for suspicion are established and an internal STR is reported to the designated AML/CFT compliance officer. The FI should however be able to demonstrate that this investigation is started immediately and has been ongoing continuously until the transaction is reported to the FIU. In this regard, and commensurate with the nature and size of their businesses, FIs should establish clear policies, procedures and staff training programmes pertaining to the identification, investigation and internal reporting of suspicious transactions (including attempted transactions), and the degree and extent of investigations that are appropriate prior to the internal reporting of a suspicious transaction (also see [Section 7.2, Identification of Suspicious Transactions](Section 7.2, Identification of Suspicious Transactions)). These policies and procedures should be documented, approved by senior management, and communicated to the appropriate levels of the organisation.
interpretation:
The regulator expects the bank to: (1) require internal reporting to the compliance officer/MLRO immediately/directly once suspicion or reasonable grounds are established; (2) report STRs to the FIU without delay once the compliance officer confirms suspicion; (3) for indicators requiring internal investigation before suspicion is established, demonstrate that investigation began immediately and continued until a reporting decision is made; and (4) establish clear, documented, senior-management-approved policies/procedures and staff training covering identification, investigation, appropriate extent of investigation, and internal reporting of suspicious transactions.

Element-by-element assessment: (1) Internal reporting to compliance officer/MLRO immediately upon suspicion -- COVERED ('The Firm's Employee must promptly notify the MLRO'). (2) External FIU reporting without delay once suspicion confirmed -- COVERED ('The MLRO must lodge the SAR with the FIU via GoAML as soon as practicable and without delay'), though 'Submit a SAR within a reasonable timeframe' language is looser than 'without delay'. (3) Distinction between obligatory indicators requiring immediate FIU reporting versus indicators requiring internal investigation first, with requirement to demonstrate investigation started immediately and continued until reporting -- NOT CLEARLY COVERED; the manual states the department 'must act immediately to conduct the necessary investigations' generically but does not distinguish obligatory/immediate-reporting indicators from those needing prior investigation, nor require documentation demonstrating investigation started immediately and continued until reporting decision. (4) Clear, documented, senior-management-approved policies/procedures and training on identification, investigation, and appropriate extent of investigation -- PARTIALLY COVERED; training section (pp.46-47) addresses general AML/CTF training but does not specifically address training on investigation of suspicious transactions and appropriate extent of investigation, nor confirm senior-management approval of these specific investigation procedures.
