clause_content:
When reporting suspicious transactions to the FIU, FIs are obliged to maintain confidentiality with regard to both the information being reported and to the act of reporting itself, and to make reasonable efforts to ensure the information and data reported are protected from access by any unauthorized person.
As part of their risk-based AML/CFT framework, and in keeping with the nature and size of their businesses, FIs, and their foreign branches or group affiliates where applicable, should establish adequate policies, procedures and controls to ensure the confidentiality and protection of information and data related to STRs. These policies, procedures and controls should be documented, approved by senior management, and communicated to the appropriate levels of the organisation.
Fls must ensure that all relevant information relating to STRs is kept confidential, with due regard to the conditions and exceptions provided for in the law, and the guiding principles for this must be established in policies and procedures. Fls need to ensure that policy and procedures are reflected in for example, appropriate access rights with regard to core systems used for case management and notifications, secure information flows and guidance/training to all staff members involved. This guidance and training is primarily important for the first-line staff who have contact with customers. It is essential that these staff know when there may be cases of suspicious transactions, what questions they have to ask the customer and which information they must not under any circumstances disclose to the customer.
It should be noted that the confidentiality requirement does not pertain to communication within the FI or its affiliated group members (foreign branches, subsidiaries, or parent company) for the purpose of sharing information relevant to the identification, prevention or reporting of suspicious transactions and/or crimes related to ML/FT.
It is a federal crime for FIs or their managers, employees or representatives, to inform a customer or any other person, whether directly or indirectly, that a report has been made or will be made, or of the information or data contained in the report, or that an investigation is under way concerning the transaction. Any person violating this prohibition is liable to a penalty of no less than AED100,000 and no more than AED500,000 and imprisonment for a term of not less than six months.
interpretation:
FIs must maintain confidentiality of reported information and the fact of reporting, protecting data from unauthorized access; establish documented, senior-management-approved policies/procedures/controls covering appropriate access rights, secure information flows, and staff guidance/training (especially for first-line customer-facing staff); ensure confidentiality rules do not restrict legitimate intra-group communication for identifying/preventing/reporting suspicious transactions; and treat tipping off as a criminal offence with specified penalties (AED100,000-500,000 fine and minimum six months imprisonment).

Several elements of the clause are covered: (1) Prohibition on tipping off customers/other persons about reports/investigations - covered (p.40-41, p.14). (2) Confidentiality of information belonging to the Compliance/AML department, including access restrictions - covered (p.14-15, 'complete confidentiality... prohibited for any party... to access any information'). (3) Confidentiality of SAR information itself - covered (p.42, 'Information contained in an SAR is confidential'). However, several required elements are NOT clearly evidenced in the excerpts: (a) an explicit statement that confidentiality requirements do NOT restrict intra-group communication for identifying/preventing/reporting suspicious transactions is absent from the manual; (b) a documented, senior-management-approved policy/procedure specifically covering 'appropriate access rights' and 'secure information flows' for STR confidentiality (beyond general department confidentiality) is not explicitly shown; (c) staff guidance/training specifically targeted at first-line customer-facing staff regarding tipping-off/confidentiality is not explicitly documented (training section on p.47-48 covers general AML training but does not call out first-line customer-facing staff specifically); (d) the specific penalty figures (AED100,000-500,000 fine, minimum six months imprisonment) for tipping off are not stated in the manual - it only says 'considered a crime' and 'will be held totally responsible' without citing the specific penalty range.
policy_extract: All  DIFC employees and contract workers are prohibited from notifying clients or any other person or other related parties that there is an investigation, report, or any related information that has been provided or will be submitted to the Financial Investigation Unit (FIU), or whether there is an internal investigation in progress or has been made in regards to a suspicion of activities or a customer.
Tipping off the customer or any other party of suspicion is considered a crime and the violator will be held totally responsible.
The Department has all the necessary power to access relevant information, records, technical systems, and data while performing its duties and responsibilities.

The Compliance / AML department has complete confidentiality to perform its duties, and it is prohibited for any party inside the  DIFC or any external party to access any information that belongs to the unit, including non-dealing lists, lists of tasks carried out, unblocking of accounts, asset freezing and unfreezing, and all information related to its work tasks.

DIFC employees are reminded that in accordance with Federal AML legislation, firms or any of their Employees must not disclose, directly or indirectly, to the Customer or to any other person that they have reported, or are intending to report, a suspicious transaction. They also must not disclose information contained in an SAR or the fact that a suspicious transaction is being investigated

Information contained in an SAR is confidential.  DIFC is protected from any criminal, civil or administrative liability which may result from providing the required information in an SAR which has been submitted in good faith.

clause_title: Protection against Liability for Reporting Persons
clause_content: Fls, as well as their board members, employees and authorised representatives, are protected by the relevant articles of the AML-CFT Law and AML-CFT Decision from any administrative, civil or criminal liability resulting from their good-faith performance of their statutory obligation to report suspicious activity to the FIU. This is also the case even if they did not know precisely what the underlying criminal activity was, and regardless of whether illegal activity actually occurred. However, it should be noted that such protections do not extend to the unlawful disclosure to the customer or any other person, whether directly or indirectly, that they have reported or intend to report a suspicious transaction, or of the information or data the report contains, or that an investigation is being conducted in relation to the transaction.
interpretation:
The regulator expects the bank's policy to inform staff/board/authorised representatives that they are protected from administrative, civil, or criminal liability for good-faith SAR reporting (even absent full knowledge of the underlying crime), while clarifying that this protection does not cover unlawful disclosure (tipping off) of the report, its contents, or the investigation.

Element 1 (protection from liability for good-faith reporting): Covered - the manual states 'DIFC is protected from any criminal, civil or administrative liability which may result from providing the required information in an SAR which has been submitted in good faith' (p.42) and that employees reporting an STR 'will not be held liable whether the suspicion is proven true or not, as long as the report has been made and sent in good faith' (p.14). However, this protection is stated as applying to the entity/employee generally without explicitly extending it to board members and authorised representatives, and without the specific clarification that protection applies 'even without knowledge of the precise underlying criminal activity or whether illegal activity actually occurred.' Element 2 (exclusion for unlawful disclosure/tipping off): Covered - the manual clearly states tipping off is a criminal offence and disclosure of SAR/investigation to customer or others is prohibited (pp.40-42). Overall, Element 2 is fully covered but Element 1 is only partially covered since board members and authorised representatives are not explicitly named as protected parties, and the 'even without knowledge of underlying criminal activity' nuance is absent.
policy_extract: Information contained in an SAR is confidential.  DIFC is protected from any criminal, civil or administrative liability which may result from providing the required information in an SAR which has been submitted in good faith.
The employee who reports an STR will not be held liable whether the suspicion is proven true or not, as long as the report has been made and sent in good faith.

‘Tipping off’ is a criminal offence which is committed when something is said or done which informs the suspect that they are under suspicion of acquiring, retaining, using or controlling the proceeds of crime, thereby prejudicing

DIFC employees are reminded that in accordance with Federal AML legislation, firms or any of their Employees must not disclose, directly or indirectly, to the Customer or to any other person that they have reported, or are intending to report, a suspicious transaction.

clause_title: Handling of Transactions and Business Relationships after Filing of STRs
clause_content:
Once a Suspicious Transaction or other suspicious information related to a Customer or Business Relationship has been reported to the FIU, there are two immediate consequences:
* FIs are obliged to follow the instructions, if any, of the FIU in relation to both the specific transaction and to the business relationship in general.
* The Customer or Business Relationship should immediately be classified as a High Risk Customer and appropriate risk-based enhanced due diligence and ongoing monitoring procedures should be implemented in order to mitigate the associated ML/FT risks (see Sections [6.4, Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) Measures](6.4), especially [6.4.2, EDD Measures for High-Risk Customers or Transactions](6.4.2), and [6.3.5 Ongoing Monitoring of the Business Relationship](6.3.5)). It is however not required to terminated the relationship.
Further guidance on both of these topics is provided below.
interpretation:
Following the filing of an STR/SAR, the FI must follow FIU instructions, must not terminate the relationship simply because a report was filed, must classify the customer as High Risk with EDD/ongoing monitoring, must avoid tipping off while managing timing of transactions, and where no FIU feedback is received within a reasonable time must document its decision rationale (reassessing risk, enhanced CDD, enhanced background investigation, additional monitoring/control measures such as documentation requirements, product/service restrictions, transaction limits) with senior management approval covering conditions, duration, removal requirements and implementation roles.

Several discrete elements of clause 7.10 are covered, but many are not: (1) COVERED - FIU may instruct DIFC on relationship handling, and DIFC follows those instructions (p.42). (2) COVERED - non-termination absent logical/unavoidable reason (DO NOT list, p.42), consistent with 'termination not required'. (3) PARTIAL - avoiding tipping off is addressed generally (CDD/tipping off, p.41) but not specifically tied to delay tactics during the FIU-feedback-waiting period. (4) NOT COVERED - no mandatory classification of the reported customer/relationship as 'High Risk' with EDD/ongoing monitoring specifically tied to STR filing; general EDD/CADD language exists but not linked to this trigger. (5) NOT COVERED - no guidance on confidentiality of FIU instructions being restricted to certain senior management/board members. (6) NOT COVERED - no specific list of delay techniques (citing operational/technical problems, lost paperwork, internal approval processes) for pending transactions awaiting FIU instruction. (7) NOT COVERED - no requirement to report additional suspicions arising during the delay period as follow-up. (8) NOT COVERED - no guidance on requesting specific FIU instructions when delay is no longer reasonably possible. (9) NOT COVERED - no guidance on determining reasonable time periods for FIU feedback based on transaction complexity/type, or on FI's discretion/no-obligation to execute transactions absent instructions. (10) NOT COVERED - no requirement to document decision rationale and implement/document additional EDD/monitoring/control measures (documentation requirements, product/service restrictions, transaction limits) with senior management approval of a plan including conditions, duration, removal requirements and implementation roles when maintaining a relationship absent FIU feedback. (11) NOT COVERED - no explicit requirement to advise FIU of intention to terminate a relationship absent official objection. None of these detailed procedural elements were found in the AML Manual excerpts provided.
policy_extract: Following the submission of the SAR, the MLRO may have an on-going dialogue with the FIU as the investigation continues as they may require more information. If  DIFC has reported a suspicion to the FIU, the FIU may instruct  DIFC directly on how to continue its business relationship, including effecting any Transaction with a Person.
DO NOT: ▪ Terminate the relationship intentionally prior to or after raising the SAR unless there is a logical and/or unavoidable reason behind such action.

If the Customer who is under suspicion expresses a wish to move the funds in question before  DIFC has received any direction from the FIU,  DIFC should immediately contact the FIU for further instructions.
If the  DIFC reasonably believes that performing CDD measures will tip off a Customer, it may choose not to pursue that process and should immediately file an external SAR.

Based on the alert investigation done by  DIFC Branch Compliance, RMs\ BMs\ Sales Representatives may be required to update customer profile/ CADD/ CTP or exercise enhance due diligence by creating CADD.

clause_content: In order for the AML/CFT framework of any organisation to be effective, it must be based on the foundation of a sound governance structure, and held together by a strong compliance culture. The governance structure should take the following into consideration: * Establish clear accountability lines and responsibilities to ensure that there is appropriate and effective oversight of staff who engage in activities which may pose a greater AML/CFT risk. * Have the mechanism to inform the board of directors (or a committee of the board) and senior management of compliance initiatives, compliance deficiencies, STRs filed and corrective actions taken; * Develop and maintain a system of reporting that provides accurate and timely information on the status of the AML/CFT program, including statistics on key elements of the program, such as the number of transactions monitored, alerts generated, cases created and STRs filed; * Develop and implement quality assurance testing programs to assess the effectiveness of the AML/CFT program's implementation and execution of its requirements. Fls should also make sure to have management structures which are accountable for clear ML/FT risk management and mitigation measures, as well as appropriate independent control functions. Implicit in both the AML-CFT Law and the AML-CFT Decision are the elements of both, concerning which additional guidance is provided in the sections below.
interpretation:
The regulator expects the FI's AML/CFT governance structure to: (1) establish clear accountability lines/responsibilities for oversight of higher-risk staff activities; (2) have mechanisms to inform the board/senior management of compliance initiatives, deficiencies, STRs filed, and corrective actions; (3) develop/maintain accurate and timely AML/CFT programme status reporting including statistics on transactions monitored, alerts, cases, and STRs filed; (4) develop and implement quality assurance testing programs to assess programme effectiveness; and (5) maintain accountable management structures for ML/FT risk management and appropriate independent control functions.

Element-by-element assessment: (1) Clear accountability lines for oversight of higher-risk staff activities -- NOT explicitly covered; the manual assigns general senior management/department responsibility but does not specifically address accountability for oversight of staff engaged in higher-AML/CFT-risk activities. (2) Mechanisms to inform board/senior management of compliance initiatives, deficiencies, STRs filed, corrective actions -- PARTIALLY covered via 'Submitting reports on the activities of the AML/CTF Department to senior management/group compliance office' and semi-annual reports to senior management with remarks/decisions (p.47-48), but no explicit board-level reporting mechanism or specific mention of STR statistics reaching the board is shown. (3) Accurate/timely AML/CFT programme status reporting including statistics on transactions monitored, alerts, cases, STRs filed -- PARTIALLY covered via 'Preparing the department's comprehensive MIS report' and periodic reports of suspicious cases (p.20-21), but statistics specifically on transactions monitored/alerts/cases/STRs are not itemized. (4) Quality assurance testing programs to assess programme effectiveness -- COVERED via 'Testing control tools on a periodic basis to ensure their effectiveness and efficiency' and quarterly RCSA testing of AML&CTF compliance requirements (pp.20-21, 47-48). (5) Accountable management structures and independent control functions -- PARTIALLY covered via Senior Management/SEO responsibilities and Internal Audit's independent periodic audit (pp.11-12, 15-16), but not framed explicitly as an 'accountable management structure for ML/FT risk management' separate from general senior management duties. Overall, several elements are only partially or not explicitly addressed in the excerpts provided.
policy_extract: The full responsibility lies with the Senior Management to ensure that the bank has effective AML/CTF measures and complying with local and international sanctions.

The Internal Audit Division must perform an independent periodic audit of the department's activities as part of the approved audit plan and document the results of the inspection and send it to the higher management.

Submitting reports on the activities of the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter Terrorist Financing Department to the senior management / group compliance office, which include statistical data in addition to identifying obstacles and challenges facing the bank to implement the requirements of AML/CTF and the necessary recommendations to improve performance and effectiveness.
Preparing the department's comprehensive MIS report.
Testing control tools on a periodic basis to ensure their effectiveness and efficiency, and developing them based on the results of periodic tests, and documenting them.

RCSA test results are reviewed by  DIFC Branch Compliance. RCSA is conducted on quarterly basis to ensure testing of compliance requirements in each business area. This includes AML&CTF compliance requirement. Issues arising out of RCSA process are discussed in BRCC. It is ensured that all outstanding issues have corrective action plans and have proper audit trails.

Relevant Persons such as  DIFC are obliged under UAE Cabinet Decision No. 10 of 2019 to prepare and submit semi-annual reports to their senior management, and to keep a copy of those reports, with senior management remarks and decisions, for any review to be conducted by Supervisory Authority (i.e. the DFSA).

clause_content: Fls are obliged to appoint a compliance officer (CO) with the appropriate competencies and experience to perform the statutory duties and responsibilities associated with this role. The AML-CFT Decision stipulates that the CO performs these duties "under his or her own responsibility", referring to the independent nature of the function and from which it should be understood that the position should be at a management level. Fls must take all appropriate steps to identify and to prevent or manage confilicts of interests between: - The FI, its' personnel including its CO, or any other representatives, including any person who is directly or indirectly associated with the organization and who has control to make decisions, and the FI's customer. - The CO and senior management of the organization including the Board of Directors. The CO must be independent and must hold a position of sufficient seniority within the organization, to ensure informed decisions are made without undue pressure to challenge decisions that are considered ill-suited, to protect the organization from possible ML/TF abuse. The MLRO's independence of judgement is required to be free from conflicts of interest, whether it is pecuniary or otherwise. The AML-CFT Decision further provides that the appointment of a person to the position of CO requires the prior consent of the relevant Supervisory Authority. Some FIs might also have appointed a Money Laundering Reporting Officer (MLRO). In determining the competencies, level of experience, and organizational reporting structures that are appropriate for their COs, FIs should take several factors into consideration, including but not limited to: * The results of the NRA and any topical risk assessment * The nature, size, complexity, and risk profile of their industries and businesses, as well as those associated with the products and services they offer and the markets and customer segments they serve; * The organisation's governance framework and management structure, with particular consideration given to the independent nature of compliance as a control function; * The specific duties and responsibilities of the CO's role (described below). Where appropriate, FIs may also consider engaging in dialogue with Supervisory Authorities, professional associations in their sectors, and industry peers, in relation to the competencies, experience, and governance structures that make for an effective compliance officer and an effective AML/CFT programme.
interpretation:
The regulator expects FIs to: (1) appoint a Compliance Officer/MLRO with appropriate competencies and experience to perform statutory duties at a management level, (2) ensure the CO performs duties independently under his/her own responsibility, (3) take appropriate steps to identify and prevent/manage conflicts of interest both between the FI/its personnel and customers, and between the CO and senior management/Board, (4) ensure the CO's independence, sufficient seniority, and freedom from pecuniary or other conflicts of interest, (5) obtain prior consent of the relevant Supervisory Authority before appointing the CO, and (6) consider NRA/topical risk assessment results, business nature/size/complexity/risk profile, governance framework, and CO role duties when determining competencies, experience and reporting lines, with optional dialogue with Supervisory Authorities/industry peers.

Element-by-element coverage: (1) Appointment with DFSA prior consent -- COVERED ('Appointing the Head Compliance (MLRO) after obtaining DFSA's approval to the appointment'). (2) Independence of the CO/department -- COVERED ('The department has complete independence...no other party...has the authority to interfere'; direct reporting to SEO). (3) Conflict of interest prevention for CO/staff -- PARTIALLY COVERED ('No delegation should be appointed to the Head compliance or any employees...that may lead to a conflict of interest') but this addresses task-delegation conflicts only, not the broader requirement to identify/prevent conflicts between FI/personnel and customers, nor specifically between CO and senior management/Board (pecuniary or otherwise). (4) Appropriate competencies/experience for statutory duties at management level -- NOT COVERED; no language specifying required competencies, experience, or seniority criteria for the CO role. (5) Consideration of NRA/topical risk assessment results, business nature/size/complexity/risk profile, governance framework, and CO role duties when determining competencies/experience/reporting structure -- NOT COVERED; no such determination framework is described in the excerpts. (6) Optional dialogue with Supervisory Authorities/professional associations/industry peers -- NOT COVERED (though this is an optional element, not core to compliance).
policy_extract: Appointing the Head Compliance (Money Laundering Reporting Officer, MLRO) after obtaining DFSA’s approval to the appointment in accordance with the regulatory requirements.

The department has complete independence in relation to the investigation of Anti-Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing cases, local and international sanctions and no other party in the DIFC has the authority to interfere in the department's decisions regarding suspicious cases and reporting them.

No delegation should be appointed to the Head compliance or any employees in the department to perform any tasks that may lead to a conflict of interest between those tasks and the tasks of their job.
Head Compliance reports directly to the SEO DIFC Branch.

clause_content: The specific tasks of the CO are detailed in the relevant provisions of the AML-CFT Decision. In general, the CO will collaborate with the relevant Supervisory Authority and the FIU to ensure that these can perform their respective duties. The CO's tasks can be grouped broadly into the following categories: * ML/FT Reporting. The compliance officer is FI's officer in charge of reviewing, scrutinizing and reporting STRs. In this capacity, the CO is ultimately responsible for the detection of transactions related to the crimes of money laundering and the financing of terrorism and of illegal organisations, for reporting suspicions to the FIU, and for cooperating with the Competent Authorities in relation to the performance of their duties in regard to AML/CFT. - __AML/CFT Programme Management.__ The CO should ensure the quality, strength and effectiveness of the FI's AML/CFT programme. As such, the CO should be a stakeholder with respect to the FI's ML/FT business risk assessment, and the overarching AML/CFT risk mitigation framework, including its AML/CFT policies, controls and CDD measures. The CO is in charge of informing and reporting to senior management on the level of compliance and report on that to the relevant Supervisory Authority. - __AML/CFT Training and Development.__ The CO is responsible for helping to establish and maintain a strong and effective AML/CFT compliance culture within the FI. This duty includes working with senior management and other internal and external stakeholders to ensure that the FI's staff are well-qualified, well-trained, well-equipped, and well-aware of their responsibility to combat the threat posed by ML/FT.
interpretation: The regulator expects the bank's AML/CTF Compliance Officer (Head of Compliance/MLRO) to have documented responsibilities covering three groupings: (1) ML/FT reporting - reviewing/scrutinising/reporting STRs, ultimate responsibility for detection and reporting to the FIU, and cooperating with Competent Authorities; (2) AML/CFT Programme Management - ensuring the programme's quality, strength and effectiveness, acting as a stakeholder in business risk assessment and risk mitigation, and informing/reporting to senior management and the Supervisory Authority on compliance levels; and (3) AML/CFT Training and Development - establishing a strong compliance culture and ensuring staff are well-qualified, trained and aware of their ML/FT responsibilities.
policy_extract:
6.8 Responsibility as MLRO
• Establishing the necessary procedures and developing the systems that ensures the monitoring of all transactions in order to identify activities that may involve money laundering and terrorist financing.
• Establishing a process to receive suspicious transaction reports related to money laundering and terrorist financing from all the different business units in the DIFC.
Sending communications, detailed studies and copies of documents of suspicious cases after MLRO approval to the Financial Investigation Unit (FIU).

Establishing procedures to ensure that the DIFC's senior management receive a periodic update on the effectiveness of regulatory controls related to Anti-Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing and adherence to local and international sanctions.

Setting procedures that guarantee the implementation of the Risk-Based Approach Policy and assessing the risks of customers, products, services, channels and countries from the Anti- Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing perspective.
Overseeing the development of training materials related to Anti-Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing and sanctions and the training plan for all DIFC employees.

Ensuring that an appropriate training program is prepared to cover the current AML/CTF regulations, and local and international sanctions and that it is provided to all members of Senior Management and Employees.

clause_content: In order for their ML/FT risk assessment and AML/CFT mitigation measures to be effective, FIs should ensure that their employees have a clear understanding of the ML/FT risks that the FI is exposed to and can exercise sound judgment, both when adhering to the FI's AML/CFT risk mitigation measures and when identifying suspicious transactions. Furthermore, due to the ever-evolving nature of ML/FT risks, FIs should ensure that their employees are kept up to date on an ongoing basis in relation to emerging ML/FT typologies and new internal and external risks. . Depending on the nature, size and level of complexity of an FI, an FI should also screen staff to ensure high standards when hiring employees. Thus, to ensure a high level of competence and AML/CFT programme effectiveness, FIs should formulate and implement appropriate policies, procedures and controls with regard to staff screening and training. An effective training program should not only explain the relevant AML/CFT laws and regulations, but also cover the institutions' policies and procedures used to mitigate ML/FT risks, scope of target employees such as but not limited: * Customer-facing staff. * AML/CFT compliance staff. * Senior management and board of directors These measures should be applied across organisations and financial groups, including their foreign branches and majority-owned subsidiaries. Examples of some of the factors that should be considered when determining appropriate staff screening and training measures include, but are not limited to: * The results of the NRA and any topical risk assessment * The nature, size, complexity, and risk profile of FIs' sectors and businesses, as well as those associated with the products and services they offer and the markets and customer segments they serve; * Effective screening and selection methods in relation the AML/CFT cultural compatibility of their employment candidates; * Assessment of staff AML/CFT competency in relation to training and development needs; * The type, frequency, structure, content, and delivery channels of AML/CFT training programmes and development opportunities; * The effective identification, deployment and management of both internal and external training resources; * Appropriate methods and tools for assessing the effectiveness of staff hiring, training, and development programmes, including screening procedures to ensure high standards when hiring employees.
interpretation:
The regulator expects FIs to have (1) documented staff screening policies for hiring with high standards, (2) training programs covering AML/CFT laws and institutional policies targeted at customer-facing staff, AML/CFT compliance staff, and senior management/board, (3) application of these measures group-wide including foreign branches/subsidiaries, and (4) a defined methodology for determining training content/frequency/structure/delivery based on risk factors (NRA results, business risk profile, staff competency assessment, effectiveness assessment tools) as well as effective screening/selection methods for cultural compatibility.

Element-by-element assessment: (1) Employee understanding of ML/FT risks and sound judgment/suspicious transaction identification -- COVERED (training aims to enhance ability to identify typologies/patterns, p.47). (2) Keeping employees updated on emerging typologies/risks -- COVERED ('inform them about any updates in the fields of money laundering, terrorist financing and sanctions'). (3) Screening staff for high standards when hiring -- NOT COVERED; no staff screening/vetting-at-hiring policy or procedure is described anywhere in the excerpts, only training obligations before employees 'start working'. (4) Training targeted at customer-facing staff, AML/CFT compliance staff, and senior management/board -- PARTIALLY COVERED; the manual lists Front-liners, Relationship Managers, Compliance, AML, Payment/Trade Operations, and 'responsible senior branch management' but does not explicitly reference the Board of Directors. (5) Application across organisation/financial group including foreign branches/majority-owned subsidiaries -- NOT COVERED; no group-wide/foreign-branch/subsidiary application language found for training/screening in these excerpts (only unrelated group-wide language appears re: AML/CTF requirements observance issues at pp.49-50, not training/screening specifically). (6) Factors for determining appropriate measures: NRA/topical risk assessment results -- NOT directly linked to training design in these excerpts (NRA is referenced elsewhere for CRA/business risk assessment, not specifically for staff training determination); business nature/size/complexity/risk profile -- PARTIALLY addressed via 'Frequency to be determined by the level of risk of the business groups' and considering products/services; effective screening/selection methods for cultural compatibility -- NOT COVERED; staff competency assessment for training needs -- PARTIALLY COVERED via 'Carrying out the necessary tests to assess the extent of the employees' understanding', though this is testing after training rather than a competency assessment to determine training needs; training programme type/frequency/structure/content/delivery -- PARTIALLY COVERED (frequency and content criteria given, but no explicit structure/delivery method or type discussion); internal/external training resource management -- NOT COVERED explicitly; effectiveness assessment methods/tools including screening procedures -- PARTIALLY COVERED via testing employees' understanding, but no broader effectiveness assessment methodology or staff screening procedure evaluation. Overall: staff screening for hiring, group-wide/foreign branch application, cultural-compatibility screening, and NRA-linked training design are missing from the AML Manual excerpts provided.
policy_extract: As per the Anti-Money Laundering Law and UAE cabinet decisions,  DIFC in coordination with training department has prepared continuous training and awareness programs for the  DIFC employees in general and the department employees in particular to improve their knowledge of the principles of due diligence and knowing customers, and to inform them about any updates in the fields of money laundering, terrorist financing and sanctions to enhance their ability to identify those typologies and their patterns and how to address them

1. The programs are designed based on the responsibility of the concerned employees (for example Front-liners, Relationship Managers, Compliance and the Anti-Money Laundering, Payment Operations and Trade Operations, etc.).
2. Take the bank's products and services into consideration (for example, new products and services, and new patterns).
3. Frequency to be determined by the level of risk of the business groups
4. All employees must be educated and informed on the importance of Anti-Money Laundering and Counter Terrorist Financing policies before they start working
5. Carrying out the necessary tests to assess the extent of the employees' understanding of the field of Anti-Money Laundering and Counter Terrorist Financing.
6. Training programs shall include the different levels of employees in the bank, including responsible senior branch management.
7. Preparing awareness programs for Anti-Money Laundering, Counter Terrorist Financing and Sanctions.

8. The bank must also educate all employees of their responsibilities, their personal duties and the penalties that they may be subject to under the law if they fail to comply with the relevant requirements as stipulated in the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter Terrorist Financing Laws.

clause_content: When an FI is part of a group, the FI is obliged to implement appropriate group-wide AML/CFT programmes, and to apply them in relation to all branches and majority-owned subsidiaries of the financial group. The specific requirements that must be met by FIs with respect to their foreign branches and majority-owned subsidiaries are set out in the relevant provisions of the AML-CFT Decision, and reflect those to which FIs are subject within the State. In meeting these obligations with regard to their branches and majority-owned subsidiaries in foreign countries, Fls, and in particular Fls that are members of financial groups, should ensure that the measures they apply are consistent with the requirements of the AML-CFT Law and AML-CFT Decision. In this regard, Fls should establish appropriate policies and procedures for the exchange and sharing of data and information, including those required for the purposes of CDD and ML/FT risk management, between the foreign branches and subsidiaries and the head office, for the purpose of combating the crimes of money laundering and the financing of terrorism and of illegal organisations, and for reporting suspicious transactions. In situations where these measures are not possible due to legislative or regulatory restrictions in the foreign countries in which their branches and majority-owned subsidiaries operate, FIs (including those which are members of Financial Groups) should implement the necessary additional measures, commensurate with the nature and size of their businesses, that will enable them to manage and mitigate appropriately the ML/FT risks that relate to their foreign operations. Examples of some of the measures that should be considered include but are not limited to: * Assessing the effectiveness of foreign branches and majority-owned subsidiaries' AML/CFT measures, including evaluating such factors as the comprehensiveness and quality of their policies, procedures and controls, and performing gap analyses in relation to the requirements of the AML-CFT Law and AML-CFT Decision; * Establishing clear policies, procedures and controls in relation to the type and extent of access which managers and employees of foreign branches and majority-owned subsidiaries have to the FIs' IT and operational systems, including CDD and transaction processing systems; * Establishing clear policies, procedures and controls in relation to the type and extent of access which customers and Business Relationships of foreign branches and majority-owned subsidiaries have to the FIs' products, services and transactional processing capabilities; * Establishing clear policies, procedures and controls in relation to the type of CDD and transaction-related information, data, and analysis FIs accept from their foreign branches and majority-owned subsidiaries in relation to customer or Business Relationship referrals, and the extent of their reliance on such information (see [Section 6.6, Reliance on a Third Party]); * Implementing service-level agreements, clearly setting out the roles and responsibilities of the parties and specifying the nature of the CDD and record-keeping requirements to be fulfilled in relation to customer or Business Relationship referrals; * Establishing protocols for the certification by the foreign branches and subsidiaries of documents and other records pertaining to the CDD measures undertaken in relation to customer or Business Relationship referrals. In particular, in cases in which the minimum AML/CFT requirements of host countries in which Fls maintain foreign operations are less strict than those of the State, Fls should take the necessary measures to ensure that their foreign branches and/or majority-owned subsidiaries in those countries implement requirements consistent with those of the State, to the extent permitted by the laws and regulations of the host countries. If such host countries do not permit the proper implementation of the AML/CFT requirements consistent with those of the State, Fls should apply appropriate additional measures to manage and mitigate the ML/FT risks (including but not limited to those described above). They should also inform the relevant Supervisory Authorities of the circumstances and comply with any additional supervisory actions, controls, or requirements of the Competent Authorities of the State (up to and including, if requested, terminating their operations in the host countries).
interpretation:
The regulator expects FIs that are part of a group to: (1) implement a group-wide AML/CFT programme applied consistently across all branches and majority-owned subsidiaries; (2) establish policies/procedures for information sharing (CDD and ML/FT risk data) between foreign branches/subsidiaries and head office for combating ML/FT and reporting STRs; (3) where foreign legislative/regulatory restrictions prevent such sharing, implement additional compensating measures (e.g., effectiveness assessments/gap analyses of foreign branch AML/CFT measures, IT/operational access policies, customer/product access policies, CDD/transaction information acceptance and reliance policies, SLAs for referrals, certification protocols for CDD documents); and (4) where host country requirements are less strict, ensure foreign branches/subsidiaries apply the home country's (UAE) higher standard to the extent permitted, apply additional risk mitigation measures where not permitted, inform the Supervisory Authority, and comply with additional supervisory actions including possible termination of host country operations if directed.

Element 1 (group-wide AML/CFT programme applied to all branches/majority-owned subsidiaries): Not addressed in excerpts - the manual is written from the perspective of a single DIFC branch reporting to a 'Head Office'/'Compliance Group', implying it is itself a branch of a group, but there is no policy language establishing a group-wide programme that the branch imposes on its own subsidiaries/branches. clause_content: A robust and independent audit function is a key component to a well-functioning governance structure and an effective AML/CFT framework. FIs are obliged to have in place an independent audit function to test the effectiveness and adequacy of their internal polices, controls and procedures relating to combating the crimes of money laundering and the financing of terrorism and of illegal organisations. In this regard, FIs should ensure that their independent audit function is appropriately staffed and organized, and that it has the requisite competencies and experience to carry out its responsibilities effectively, commensurate with the ML/FT risks to which the FIs are exposed, and with the nature and size of their businesses. It should be noted that, while most FIs are expected to have the capacity to meet these requirements internally, depending on the nature and size of their businesses, some FIs (particularly smaller ones) may not necessarily have the resources to maintain a fully functioning and effective internal audit unit. In such cases, those FIs should ensure that they take adequate measures to obtain the necessary capabilities from qualified external sources. They should also ensure that they have in place adequate internal capabilities to provide sufficient coordination with and oversight of any external resources they may utilise, and that such external resources are adequately regulated and supervised by relevant Competent Authorities. Fls should ensure that the periodic inspection and testing of all aspects of their AML/CFT compliance programmes, including ML/FT business risk assessment and AML/CFT mitigation measures, and CDD policies, procedures and controls, is incorporated into their regular audit plans. They should also ensure that all their branches and the subsidiaries in which they hold a majority interest, whether domestic or foreign, are part of an independent audit testing programme that covers the effectiveness and adequacy of their internal AML/CFT polices, controls and procedures. Some of the factors FIs should consider in determining the appropriate frequency and extent of audit testing of their AML/CFT programmes by their independent audit functions include but are not limited to: * The results of the NRA and any topical risk assessment; * The nature, size, complexity, and geographic scope of the FIs' businesses, and the results of their ML/TF business risk assessments; * The risk profile associated with the products and services they offer and the markets and customer segments they serve; * The frequency of supervision and inspection by, and the nature of the feedback (including the imposition of administrative sanctions) they receive from, Supervisory Authorities, relative to enhancing the effectiveness of their AML/CFT measures; * Internal and external developments in relation to ML/FT risks, as well as developments pertaining to the management and operations of the FIs. The scope of such audits should include but not be limited to: * Examine the adequacy of AML/CFT and CDD policies, procedures and processes, and whether they comply with regulatory requirements. * Assess training adequacy, including its comprehensiveness, accuracy of materials, training schedule, attendance tracking and escalation procedures for lack of attendance. * Review all the aspects of any AML/CFT compliance function that have been outsourced to third parties, including the qualifications of the personnel, the contract and the performance and reputation of the company. * Review case management and STR systems, including an evaluation of the research and referral of unusual transactions, and a review of policies, procedures and processes for referring unusual or suspicious activity from all business lines to the personnel responsible for investigating unusual activity
interpretation:

The audit plan's frequency/scope should be risk-based (informed by NRA/topical risk assessment, business nature/size/complexity, product/customer risk profile, supervisory feedback, and internal/external risk developments), and the audit scope must specifically cover: (1) adequacy of AML/CFT/CDD policies and regulatory compliance, (2) training programme adequacy (comprehensiveness, accuracy, schedule, attendance tracking, escalation), (3) outsourced AML/CFT compliance functions (personnel qualifications, contracts, performance, reputation) where applicable, and (4) case management/STR systems including research/referral of unusual transactions.

Element-by-element assessment: (1) Existence of independent audit function - COVERED: the Manual states Internal Audit performs independent periodic audits covering Compliance/AML-CTF and documents results to senior management (pp.11-12, 49-50). (2) Staffing/competency commensurate with risk, and use of qualified external sources for smaller FIs with internal oversight - NOT COVERED: no mention of audit team staffing/competency requirements or provisions for outsourcing audit capability to qualified external providers with internal coordination/oversight. (3) Coverage of all branches/majority-owned subsidiaries domestic and foreign - NOT COVERED: no explicit statement that audit scope extends to all branches and majority-owned subsidiaries (domestic/foreign). (4) Factors determining audit frequency/extent (NRA results, business nature/size/complexity, product/customer risk profile, supervisory feedback, risk developments) - NOT COVERED: the Manual does not specify how audit frequency or scope is determined based on these risk factors. (5) Audit scope specifics: (a) examining AML/CFT/CDD policy adequacy and regulatory compliance - PARTIALLY COVERED (generic statement that audit 'covers Compliance and AML&CTF requirements' but no detail on assessing policy/procedure adequacy specifically); (b) assessing training adequacy (comprehensiveness, accuracy, schedule, attendance tracking, escalation) - NOT COVERED: no mention of audit reviewing training programme adequacy; (c) reviewing outsourced AML/CFT compliance functions (personnel qualifications, contract, performance, reputation) - NOT COVERED: no mention in the audit section; (d) reviewing case management/STR systems including research/referral of unusual transactions - NOT COVERED: no mention of audit function reviewing STR/case management systems specifically. Overall, while the existence of an independent internal audit function reviewing AML/CTF is established, the detailed scope requirements, risk-based frequency determination, external-sourcing provisions for smaller FIs, and coverage across branches/subsidiaries are missing from the AML Manual excerpts.

clause_content: A cornerstone of any sound governance structure, including those related to AML/CFT compliance, is senior management involvement and accountability. The members of an FI's senior management (together with the members of the board of directors in those organisations that have one) are ultimately responsible for the quality, strength and effectiveness of the FI's AML/CFT framework, as well as for the robustness of its compliance culture. In this regard, an FI's senior management should set the ML/FT risk appetite and a proper "tone at the top," by demonstrating their commitment to ensuring an effective AML/CFT compliance programme is in place, and by clearly articulating their expectations with regard to the responsibilities and accountability of all staff members in relation to it. Under the AML/CFT legal and regulatory framework of the UAE, the senior management of all FIs are responsible for performing certain functions related to the assessment, management and mitigation of the ML/FT risks to which their organisations are exposed. These responsibilities can be grouped broadly into categories which include: • Implementation of governance, control, and operating systems. These include such elements as: – Appointing a qualified compliance officer in line with the requirements of the relevant Supervisory Authority; – Ensuring a robust and effective independent audit function is in place; – Putting in place and monitoring the implementation of adequate management and information systems, internal controls, and policies, procedures to mitigate risks. • Approval of internal policies, procedures and controls. These include such elements as the FI's overall ML/FT risk appetite as well as the framework of AML/CFT policies, procedures and controls related to areas such as: – Identification, assessment, understanding, management and mitigation of ML/FT risks; – Performance, review and updating of CDD (including EDD and SDD) measures; – Identification and implementation of indictors to identify suspicious transactions; – Record retention and data protection; – Staff screening, training and development. • Oversight of the AML/CFT compliance programme. This includes such elements as: – Reviewing and providing comments in relation to the compliance officer's semi-annual reports to the relevant Supervisory Authority; – Approving the establishment and continuance of High Risk Customer Business Relationships and their associated transactions, including those with PEPs; – Approving the establishment and continuance of Business Relationships involving high- risk countries; – Approving the establishment and continuance of relationships with correspondent institutions; – Ensuring the adequate application of the appropriate components of the AML/CFT compliance programme to all branches and majority-owned subsidiaries, including those operating in foreign jurisdictions. • Application of the directives of Competent Authorities. This includes such elements as: – Applying the directives of Competent Authorities for implementing UN Security Council decisions under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations, and other related directives, including Cabinet Decision (74) of 2020 Regarding Terrorism Lists Regulation and Implementation of UN Security Council Resolutions On the Suppression and Combating of Terrorism, Terrorists Financing & Proliferation of Weapons of Mass Destruction, and Related Resolutions; – Implementing CDD measures defined by the National Committee for Combating Money Laundering and the Financing of Terrorism and Illegal Organisations, regarding High Risk Countries.
interpretation:
The regulator expects the internal AML Manual to explicitly document that senior management (and board, where applicable) bears ultimate responsibility for the AML/CFT framework's quality and effectiveness and the compliance culture, and to enumerate specific senior management responsibilities across four categories: (1) implementation of governance/control systems including appointing a qualified Compliance Officer, ensuring an independent audit function, and adequate MIS/controls; (2) approval of internal policies/procedures including risk appetite, ML/FT risk framework, CDD/EDD/SDD procedures, suspicious transaction indicators, record retention/data protection, and staff screening/training; (3) oversight of the compliance programme including reviewing CO semi-annual reports, approving high-risk/PEP/high-risk country/correspondent relationships, and ensuring programme application across all branches/subsidiaries; and (4) applying directives of Competent Authorities including UNSC Chapter VII decisions/Cabinet Decision 74 and NAMLCFTFC high-risk country CDD measures.

Element-by-element assessment: (1) Overall senior management responsibility for AML/CTF framework effectiveness - COVERED ('The full responsibility lies with the Senior Management to ensure that the bank has effective AML/CTF measures...'). (2) Setting risk appetite / tone at the top - NOT explicitly covered; no clause found stating senior management sets ML/FT risk appetite. (3) Appointing a qualified CO - NOT explicitly covered as a senior management duty (MLRO appointment is mentioned but not framed as a senior management responsibility to appoint a 'qualified' CO). (4) Ensuring independent audit function - PARTIALLY covered (Internal Audit performs periodic audits, reported to higher management, but not framed as senior management 'ensuring' this function). (5) Adequate MIS/controls - NOT explicitly tied to senior management responsibility in excerpts. (6) Approval of internal policies/procedures (risk appetite, ML/FT risk framework, CDD/EDD/SDD, suspicious transaction indicators, record retention/data protection, staff screening/training) - NOT found as senior management approval requirement in excerpts (policy approval responsibilities are attributed to Compliance/AML department, e.g. section 6.14, not senior management). (7) Reviewing CO semi-annual reports - COVERED ('Relevant Persons...are obliged...to prepare and submit semi-annual reports to their senior management...with senior management remarks and decisions'). (8) Approving High-Risk Customer/PEP relationships - COVERED ('Senior Management approval is required for High-Risk customers from an AML/CTF perspective'). (9) Approving high-risk country relationships - COVERED (KYC update approval for high-risk country financial institutions requires senior management approval, correspondent banking section). (10) Approving correspondent relationships - COVERED ('The approval of the senior management is required to establish the correspondent banking relationships'). (11) Ensuring programme application to all branches/subsidiaries including foreign - NOT explicitly covered in excerpts. (12) Applying UNSC Chapter VII/Cabinet Decision 74 directives - COVERED at an institutional level but not explicitly framed as a senior management responsibility. (13) Implementing High Risk Country CDD measures per NAMLCFTFC - COVERED partially via high-risk country EDD language but not explicitly tied to senior management application of NAMLCFTFC-defined measures. Overall, several oversight/approval elements (high-risk/PEP/correspondent/high-risk country approvals, semi-annual report review) are well covered, but risk appetite setting, CO appointment qualification, MIS/controls adequacy, and explicit senior management approval of policies/procedures (CDD/EDD/SDD, STR indicators, record retention, staff screening/training) are missing or only found attributed to the Compliance Department rather than Senior Management in the excerpted text.

clause_content: Some FIs may operate as small or mid-sized businesses, without large staff organisations or sophisticated IT infrastructures. In such cases, individual managers and employees may often be called upon to undertake multiple roles and responsibilities in the course of day-to-day business activities, and it may be difficult at times to maintain a clear separation of duties or functions. While an FI's small size does not in any way exempt it from fulfilling its obligations under the AML-CFT Law and the AML-CFT Decision, and without prejudice to guidance provided in the previous sections, the following additional considerations are of particular importance to small and mid-sized FIs. * In situations in which the responsibilities of the AML/CFT compliance officer are delegated to a manager or staff member who also has other responsibilities, FIs should undertake their best efforts to ensure that the designated AML/CFT compliance officer does not have day-to-day responsibility for sales and/or customer business relationship management. * When an adequate separation of responsibilities is not possible due to the small size of an FI's organisation, FIs should take the necessary steps to ensure that operational and AML/CFT policies and procedures (particularly those pertaining to CDD, the identification and reporting of Suspicious Transactions, and the monitoring and updating of required High Risk Country CDD measures, and Local and Sanctions Lists—see Sections [6, Customer Due Diligence (CDD)], [6.4.3 Requirements for High-Risk Countries], and [10, International Financial Sanctions]) are clearly formulated, documented, and adhered to during the establishment and ongoing monitoring of business relationships and the carrying out of transactions. * In such cases, FIs should ensure that they clearly document the rationale for any policy and/or procedural exceptions they make, along with any additional AML/CFT risk mitigation measures they implement, and that these records are properly retained in accordance with the statutory record-keeping requirements (see [Section 9, Record Keeping]). FIs should also consider referring to any significant policy or procedural exceptions, along with their rationale, associated additional AML/CFT risk mitigation measures, and senior management comments, in the AML/CFT compliance officer's required semi-annual reports to the relevant Supervisory Authorities. * FIs that are unable to ensure a clear and effective separation of AML/CFT responsibilities from those related to the day-to-day management of their businesses, including but not limited to sales and customer business relationship management functions, due to the small size of their organisation should also consider taking additional measures to enhance the application of their independent audit controls (see [Section 8.4, Independent Audit Function]). Examples of such measures include but are not limited to: - Incorporating the audit of policies, procedures (particularly those pertaining to CDD, the identification of Suspicious Transactions, and the monitoring and updating of required High Risk Country CDD measures, and Local and Sanctions Lists), and records related to exceptions made to them, as part of their audit plans and/or their service-level agreements with their external providers of independent audit services; - Increasing the frequency of independent audits and random audit inspections; - Applying stricter criteria with regard to the review of past transactions, such as increasing the number of transactions reviewed for a given time period, reducing size threshold limits for transactions to be reviewed, or taking other reasonable measures in this regard.
interpretation:
The regulator expects small/mid-sized FIs to still meet all AML-CFT obligations despite limited staff/IT resources, and specifically to: (1) ensure the Compliance Officer, if given other duties, does not also hold day-to-day sales/customer relationship management responsibility; (2) where segregation of duties is not achievable due to size, ensure that core AML/CFT policies (CDD, STR, High Risk Country CDD, sanctions monitoring) are clearly formulated, documented and adhered to; (3) clearly document the rationale for any policy/procedural exceptions and additional mitigating measures, retain these per record-keeping rules, and consider referencing significant exceptions in the CO's semi-annual report to the Supervisory Authority; and (4) where clear separation of AML/CFT duties from business management is not achievable, consider enhanced independent audit measures (exception-focused audits, increased audit/inspection frequency, stricter transaction review criteria).

The excerpts do not address governance considerations for small/mid-sized institutions at all. Specifically: (1) No provision stating the CO/MLRO must not hold day-to-day sales/relationship management duties when responsibilities are combined due to small size - not found. (2) No statement that where segregation is not possible, core AML/CFT policies (CDD, STR, High Risk Country CDD, sanctions monitoring) must be clearly formulated/documented/adhered to as a compensating control for small-org structure - not found (general CDD/STR/sanctions procedures exist elsewhere in the manual but not framed as a small-org governance mitigant). (3) No requirement to document rationale for policy/procedural exceptions and retain per record-keeping rules, nor to consider referencing significant exceptions in the semi-annual report to DFSA - the semi-annual report reference exists (p.47-48) but nothing ties it to documenting exceptions arising from small-org governance gaps. (4) No provision for enhanced independent audit measures (exception-focused audits, increased audit frequency, stricter review criteria/sample sizes) specifically tied to inadequate separation of AML/CFT duties from business management - the Internal Audit section (p.49-50) covers general AML/CFT audit coverage but not this small-org contingency.

clause_title: Obligations and Timeframe for the Retention and Availability of Records
interpretation:
The regulator expects FIs to maintain comprehensive records (transactions, CDD, account files/correspondence, analysis results, risk assessment/mitigation documentation) organized to permit data analysis and transaction reconstruction, available immediately to Competent Authorities, retained for at least 5 years from the latest of several specified trigger events (relationship termination/account closure, occasional transaction completion, supervisory inspection completion, final judicial judgment, or legal entity liquidation/dissolution), with documented, senior-management-approved policies covering roles/responsibilities, record-keeping functions (logging, cataloguing, archiving, handling, transferring, destruction), physical/cyber security, and audit/QA testing.

Element-by-element review: (1) Record types (transactions, CDD, account files/correspondence, analysis results, risk assessment documentation) - COVERED, explicitly listed. (2) Organization to permit data analysis/transaction tracking - PARTIALLY COVERED, generic statement about easy reference and transaction tracking but no detail on data analysis capability requirements. (3) Availability immediately to Competent Authorities - COVERED (24hr expectation noted). (4) Sufficiency to permit reconstruction of transactions for prosecution evidence - NOT explicitly addressed; no mention of evidentiary reconstruction standard. (5) Retention period - the Manual specifies 10 years (exceeds the 5-year minimum, so compliant on duration) but the trigger events differ: it lists relationship termination/transaction conclusion/account closure/contract end, but does NOT include 'completion of a Supervisory Authority records inspection', 'issue date of a final judicial judgment', or 'liquidation/dissolution/termination of a legal person/arrangement' as retention start triggers - these specific triggers are missing in the AML Manual. (6) Documented, senior-management-approved retention policies - NOT explicitly evidenced in excerpts (no approval reference found). (7) Record-keeping roles/responsibilities for risk assessment/AML policy implementation - PARTIALLY addressed via department record-keeping duties but not tied comprehensively to record retention governance. (8) Record-keeping functional roles (logging, cataloguing, archiving, handling, transferring, destruction of expired records) - PARTIALLY COVERED; archiving mentioned generically but no destruction/handling/transferring procedures documented. (9) Physical/cyber security protections for records - NOT addressed in excerpts. (10) Audit/QA testing of record-keeping - NOT specifically addressed (general internal audit coverage exists but not focused on record-keeping QA).

clause_content: The AML-CFT Law and AML-CFT Decision oblige FIs to retain several types of records, which can be classified broadly into the following categories: * Transaction Records. This category relates to operational and statistical records, documents and information concerning all transactions executed or processed by the FI, whether domestic or international in nature. * CDD Records. This category relates to records, documents, and information about customers, their due diligence, and the investigation and analysis of their activities, and can be further divided into sub-categories such as records pertaining to: - Customer Information, including account files and business correspondence, and results of any analysis undertaken - Company Information - Reliance on Third Parties to Undertake CDD - Ongoing Monitoring of Business Relationships - Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs) Additional guidance related to these record types is provided in the following sub-sections.
interpretation:
The regulator expects FIs to retain two broad categories of records: (1) Transaction Records covering operational/statistical data on all domestic and international transactions, and (2) CDD Records, further sub-divided into: Customer Information (account files, business correspondence, analysis results), Company Information, Reliance on Third Parties for CDD, Ongoing Monitoring of Business Relationships, and Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs). Each of these sub-categories should be identifiable as a retained record type within the institution's record-keeping policy.

Element-by-element assessment: (1) Transaction Records (operational/statistical, domestic/international) - COVERED: manual references 'financial transactions... including cash transactions and money transfers' and 'account statements report'. (2) Customer Information (account files, business correspondence, analysis results) - COVERED: 'account opening files', 'correspondence, credit files', 'results of any analysis carried out'. (3) Company Information - PARTIALLY COVERED: 'entity incorporation documents' mentioned but no distinct sub-category for company-specific records (e.g., ownership structure, registration documents beyond incorporation) is clearly enumerated. (4) Reliance on Third Parties for CDD - NOT COVERED: no explicit mention in the excerpts of retaining records related to reliance on third parties for CDD purposes. (5) Ongoing Monitoring of Business Relationships - PARTIALLY COVERED: general references to 'update forms', 'field visit forms', and periodic KYC updates exist, but not explicitly framed as a 'monitoring records' retention sub-category. (6) Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs) - COVERED: explicit six-year retention requirement for SARs including internal findings, analysis and FIU communications. Overall, the manual addresses most elements but does not explicitly address record retention for reliance on third-party CDD providers, and Company Information / Ongoing Monitoring are only implicitly covered.

The excerpts contain a general record-retention requirement only for SARs (6 years) and general KYC/beneficial ownership identification obligations during onboarding, but there is no provision addressing: (1) retention obligations specific to company dissolution/liquidation/termination scenarios where the bank acts as administrator, liquidator or holds a controlling interest; (2) the specific 5-year retention period from date of dissolution/liquidation/termination for corporate documents (formation, registration, deregistration, liquidation, dissolution/expiry documents, share registers, MOA/AOA, deeds of settlement, foundation charters and amendments) and BO/shareholder/director/senior manager identification documents; (3) documented policies, procedures and controls for this scenario approved by senior management and communicated to relevant staff. None of this is found in the Internal AML Manual excerpts provided.
policy_extract: DIFC is required to maintain records of all SARs and any relevant supporting documents and information, including internal findings and analysis plus any relevant communications with the FIU for at least six years from the date on which the notification or report was made, the business relationship ends or the transaction is completed, whichever occurs last.

clause_title: Reliance on Third Parties to Undertake CDD
interpretation:
The regulator expects FIs that rely on third parties for CDD to (1) ensure copies of all CDD documents can be obtained on request without delay, (2) ensure third parties adhere to AML-CFT Decision record-keeping provisions, and (3) establish documented, senior-management-approved policies/procedures/controls for assessing, monitoring and testing the third party's record-retention framework -- covering roles/responsibilities for assessment/monitoring/testing, SLA implementation responsibilities, operational procedures for record request/transfer/security, and audit/QA testing of the third party's record-retention framework.

Element 1 (ability to obtain document copies on request without delay) - Covered: manual states DIFC 'takes adequate steps to satisfy itself that certified copies... will be available from the third party on request without delay.' Element 2 (third party adherence to record-keeping standards) - Partially covered: manual references FATF record-keeping standards for third parties in other jurisdictions but does not explicitly reference adherence to the AML-CFT Decision's specific record-keeping provisions. Element 3 (documented, senior-management-approved policies/procedures/controls for assessment, monitoring, and testing of third parties' record-retention frameworks) - Not covered: no text found describing a structured program to assess, monitor, or test third-party record-retention frameworks, nor senior management approval of such a program. Element 4 (specific factors: roles/responsibilities for assessment/monitoring/testing, SLA implementation responsibilities, operational procedures for record request/transfer/physical-cyber security, audit/QA testing of third-party's record-retention framework) - Not covered: none of these specific sub-elements appear in the excerpts.
policy_extract: It takes adequate steps to satisfy itself that certified copies of the documents used to undertake the relevant elements of CDD will be available from the third party on request without delay;
subject to requirements in relation to customer due diligence and record keeping which meet the standards set out in the FATF Recommendations; and

If  DIFC is not reasonably satisfied with the CDD undertaken by a third party,  DIFC must perform the CDD itself with respect to any deficiencies identified.  Notwithstanding reliance on a third party, it should be noted that  DIFC remains responsible for compliance with, and liable for any failure to meet,  / the CDD requirements in the DFSA AML module.

interpretation:
The regulator expects FIs to retain, as part of ongoing monitoring of business relationships, all customer records/documents generated through monitoring activity, specifically: (1) transaction review/analysis/investigation files and related correspondence; (2) customer correspondence (email, fax) and call reports/meeting minutes/recordings/transcripts/logs related to transaction analysis/investigation; (3) CDD records/documents/profiles/information gathered while reviewing/analysing/investigating transactions, plus supporting documentation including background search results on customers, beneficial owners, beneficiaries, controlling persons or counterparties; and (4) transaction handling decisions (approval/rejection records) with related analysis and correspondence.

Element-by-element review: (1) Transaction review/analysis/investigation files with related correspondence -- partially covered via 'Internal audits, self-assessment and inquiry work papers investigating suspicious or abnormal transactions' and 'results of any analysis carried out should be kept', but explicit retention of investigation-related correspondence is not clearly documented. (2) Customer correspondence (email/fax) and call reports/meeting minutes/recordings/transcripts/logs of calls related to transaction analysis/investigation -- not addressed anywhere in the excerpts; the manual only mentions general 'correspondence' and 'meeting' records for compliance corrective actions, not customer call/meeting records tied to transaction analysis. (3) CDD records/profiles/information gathered during review/analysis/investigation of transactions, including background search results on customers, beneficial owners, beneficiaries, controlling persons or counterparties -- partially covered ('All records obtained through due diligence measures... KYC documents and results of any analysis') but background-search results on beneficiaries/controlling persons/counterparties specifically are not mentioned. (4) Transaction handling decisions including approval/rejection records with related analysis and correspondence -- partially covered ('Copies of rejected transactions due to their abnormality and copies of account documentations where relationship is denied due to suspicion') but approval records and related correspondence for accepted transactions are not explicitly mentioned. Overall the manual establishes strong general record-retention requirements (10-year retention, various document categories) but does not explicitly enumerate call recordings/transcripts/logs, meeting minutes, or comprehensive transaction approval/rejection documentation with correspondence as required by this clause.

interpretation:
The regulator expects FIs to retain, for the required retention period, all records and documents related to STRs and the analysis/investigations underlying them, including: suspicious transaction indicator alerts/logs, investigations, recommendations and decisions, related correspondence; competent authority requests and correspondent bank assistance requests with their investigation files/correspondence; CDD and business relationship monitoring records/documents/information obtained during analysis or investigation of potentially suspicious transactions and associated correspondence; STR logs and statistics with related analysis/recommendations/decisions and correspondence (internal and external STRs); and notes on FIU feedback on reported STRs plus any other FIU-required actions.

Element-by-element review: (1) SAR/STR supporting records, internal findings/analysis, FIU communications - COVERED ('DIFC is required to maintain records of all SARs and any relevant supporting documents and information, including internal findings and analysis plus any relevant communications with the FIU'). (2) Records of internal reports/investigation reports/studies on suspected ML/TF/sanctions cases - COVERED ('The department maintains a record of all reports related to Anti-Money Laundering and Counterterrorist Financing, including investigation reports and studies'). (3) Records of cases/reports submitted to FIU - COVERED. (4) Records of external inquiries from regulatory authorities and correspondent banks - COVERED ('a record of all inquiries and requests related to Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing transactions received from regulatory authorities, other relevant authorities, and correspondent banks'). (5) Suspicious transaction indicator alert records/logs and specific decision records tied to alerts - NOT explicitly covered; the manual references general 'inquiry work papers investigating suspicious or abnormal transactions' but does not specifically mention alert logs, indicator alert records, or STR statistics/logs. (6) STR logs and statistics - NOT covered; no mention of maintaining STR statistics or logs distinct from case records. (7) CDD and Business Relationship monitoring records/documents obtained specifically in the course of analysing/investigating potentially suspicious transactions - NOT explicitly tied to STR investigation record-keeping (general CDD record retention exists elsewhere in the manual but not linked to STR analysis). (8) Notes on FIU feedback regarding reported STRs and other FIU-required actions - NOT explicitly covered; manual mentions FIU communications generally but does not specifically require retention of feedback notes from FIU. Overall, several core elements (SAR docs, internal reports, FIU submissions, external inquiries) are covered, but alert/indicator logs, STR statistics, CDD/monitoring records tied to STR analysis, and FIU feedback notes are not explicitly addressed, making this a partial match.
